the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally demanding. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends existing superfluid approximations and demonstrates superior performance in handling quantum fluctuations. We outline the implications of these findings for applications to non-equilibrium scenarios, such as quantum turbulence. Additionally, the study offers a comprehensive introduction to positive-P hydrodynamics, providing detailed instructions on implementing the algorithm in hydrodynamic simulations. Through numerical illustrations using an interacting quantum Hall system and various correlation functions, we highlight the scheme's advantages over the Gaussian approximation in specific regimes. Ultimately, this work aims to facilitate the adoption of this method, which currently exceeds the processing power available on supercomputers, by researchers investigating diverse and challenging many-body quantum systems across different physical platforms. This combination fuels increased trading volumes and fuels speculation that prices will continue climbing indefinitely. However, price increases cannot sustain themselves forever.

This paper introduces a mathematical model grounded in price action theory designed to anticipate local price peaks and troughs. Although price action concepts are straightforward, formulating them within a rigorous mathematical framework is complex. Our model integrates these ideas with a stochastic process known as the Wildier sawtooth process. We demonstrate how to calculate extrema using our proposed process and develop a method for estimating a local peak-to-trough ratio. These calculations rely on a world record process associated with the Wildier sawtooth mechanism, which operates under the assumption of Geometric Brownian motion within an efficient market. Additionally, we established a "selling rule" based on a local price peak-to-trough ratio, which was tested on Nasdaq data from 1971 to 2019, yielding positive results. Additionally, a "buying rule" was developed and evaluated on both Nasdaq and Israeli stock indices, also producing favorable outcomes. Overall, our findings indicate that a price peak-to-trough ratio process can effectively predict local extrema in prices.

The proposed approach requires only marginal extra effort compared to standard FGMRES usage. Furthermore, the method is broadly applicable to any system where one wishes to preserve constraints or properties characterized by a norm. The findings highlight that achieving exact property preservation across time is feasible with minimal additional cost, even when solving nonlinear systems incompletely at each step. These results also suggest potential applications in retiming existing codes to incorporate constraints into solutions across both space and time. The approach is implemented in the open-source Python package PySPRINT. PyPyCharm themes for both PyCharm and IntelliJ IDEA are available at https://github.com/pycharm-theme/pycharm-theme/releases, and the PyCharm theme can be installed via the PyPI repository using `pip install pycharm-theme`. Additional resources, including a Discord server, are hosted at https://pycharm-theme.github.io/. The project was developed with PyCharm Community Edition free trial versions available at https://www.jetbrains.com/pycharm/download/, https://www.jetbrains.com/pycharm/download/?section=download&type=community&os=win&lang=EN, and https://www.jetbrains.com/pycharm/download/?section=download&type=community&os=mac&lang=EN.

soft-tissue navigation, specifically within laparoscopic liver surgery. This process involves aligning a pre-operative CT-derived organ model with an intra-operative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy optical data, missing regions, and the deformable nature of liver tissue. We introduce a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained end-to-end to perform this pre-and post-operative liver registration. To address the challenges of incomplete and noisy surface data, we utilize volumetric slabs derived from the pre-operative organ model and the intra-operative surface data. To ensure sparse volumes align with the actual tissue surface, we apply boundary constraints to the lowest two volume slices. Our approach requires no hand-crafted features; instead, we leverage learned volume features across multiple planes to reduce dimensionality before feeding 2D data into a convolutional regression network for displacement prediction. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional image-based registration techniques, with errors remaining below the sampling density of the intra-operative surfaces. Furthermore, these low registration errors validate the end-to-end learning pipeline's efficacy, confirming its potential to support real-time liver navigation. Unlike prior methods, this technique requires only the surface data, representing a notable advancement over earlier approaches. Additionally, we offer a streamlined model variant requiring roughly one-fifth of the training time of the original model while maintaining similar performance on real data. The synthetic data generation code and models are accessible on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/AmirhosseinCNNs/NRRigidNonRigidNet.

While these vectors are highly valuable for subsequent tasks like collision avoidance and action recognition, acquiring precise annotations for LiDAR and stereo camera data is both labor-intensive and computationally demanding. To overcome this annotation barrier, we propose a solution leveraging monocular depth sequences. By applying our method to depth trajectories derived from moving objects in video, we achieve a top-scored regression result in the SOT-Bench evaluation (a benchmark for visual object tracking) using a depth-supervised pretrained model. Since our approach relies on object motion captured in depth sequences rather than dense pixel-level flow, it remains largely unsupervised. This allows it to benefit from vast amounts of video data without requiring action annotations, potentially leading to improved generalization across novel scenes and distributions. Our method, DepthMotFlow, utilizes a three-stage pipeline: (1) extracting depth sequences and identified moving objects, (2) generating motion bounding boxes, and (3) deriving 3D motion vectors for points on these bounding boxes. for automatically generating system call filtering policies tailored to containerized microservices. During runtime, Timeloops identifies which system calls a program should execute while blocking unauthorized attempts. It overcomes several limitations of current static analysis approaches, particularly in creating precise filters for interpreted languages like Python, PHP, and JavaScript. The system relies on a straightforward and robust architecture built from established, off-the-shelf technologies—including seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers—requiring fewer than 500 lines of code. We validate Timeloops by learning system call behaviors for individual services and two microservice benchmarks utilizing popular frameworks such as Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua), Apache Thrift, and databases like Redis, Memcached, and MongoDB. Additionally, Timeloops surpasses existing static analysis tools by learning system call patterns from any program, including those written in difficult-to-analyze languages. Furthermore, the system distinguishes between dynamic analysis via system call tracing and traditional bytecode instrumentation, offering tighter and more secure filters that reduce false positives in dynamic behavior learning. By significantly lowering the cost of analyzing new services, Timeloops enables the derivation of accurate system call filters through existing, proven methodologies. Crucially, the system maintains high performance with minimal overhead, utilizing efficient and secure BPF bytecode, and ensures practical deployment by supporting both standalone and Kubernetes environments. Finally, Timeloops reinforces the security of lightweight microservices by addressing threats that bypass standard Kubernetes controls, and it facilitates the development of behavioral monitors and intrusion detectors for these services. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yanaviram/timeloops. Preliminary findings of this research were presented at the 1st USENX Microservices Workshop in 2019.

where even superior teams often fail to score, creating an environment where every decision counts. Because the stakes are high in each moment, players must constantly evaluate their options based on the current state. This study analyzes the decision-making processes of professional players, specifically examining possession duration and the intensity of pressing—the action of forcing the opponent to pass under high pressure or losing possession. The analysis focuses on the 60 seconds preceding a pass, categorizing this interval into three segments based on the distance to the passer: the final 15 seconds, the middle 15 seconds, and the initial 30 seconds. Passes were evaluated for their success rate, the distance to the goal after the pass, and the speed at which pressing began. The results indicate that in the final 15 seconds before a pass, players in positions closer to the goal experience higher pressing intensity and are pressured to deliver passes that result in longer distances to the goal. Furthermore, passing success varies significantly across these positions and time intervals, with players in deeper positions achieving higher success rates in the first 30 seconds of the sequence but facing more intense pressing in the subsequent 15 seconds. Overall, the study demonstrates that pressing intensity and passing success are not uniform throughout the sequence leading up to a pass; instead, they follow opposing trends, where increased pressing intensity often correlates with improved passing success. These findings were derived from a database constructed for FC Porto's home matches during the 2017-2018 season. The paper concludes by suggesting research directions for analyzing possession duration and pressing intensity in relation to passing success, offering insights for soccer players, particularly in understanding how to balance high-intensity pressing with effective decision-making. Keywords: Soccer, Positioning, Pressing, Passing Success.

By modeling noise as additive Gaussian with spatially non-uniform standard deviations, we explore scenarios where some voters exhibit greater stochasticity than others. Simulation results are supported by analytical calculations based on a set of coupled noise-difference equations. Specifically, we identify the critical condition required for the transition from a polarized state, characterized by two distinct opinion peaks, to a single-peak state centered at zero. We further demonstrate that minimizing the average overall noise level is not sufficient to drive this transition; instead, the spatial distribution of the noise is decisive. This is because concentrating more noise on one side of the system accelerates the collapse of the positive opinion peak relative to the negative one. Additionally, we analyze the associated single-noise-difference dynamics and derive the exact critical ratio of noise standard deviations that triggers the transition. Our findings indicate that this critical ratio is approximately 0.87, which is lower than the corresponding value in the symmetric case (0.5 + 0.5 = 1). We also investigate asymmetric noise configurations where the standard deviations on both sides of the system are increased, showcasing diverse behaviors depending on the specific noise distribution. These insights are directly applicable to analyzing the dynamics of competitive relationships, such as two political candidates or firms within the same industry. An important implication of our results is that even minimal, asymmetric noise increases the probability of one side reaching zero opinion before the other. We support these conclusions with additional simulations examining noise patterns where the standard deviation follows an exponential increase or decrease. These exponential profiles allow for a broader range of critical values for the coefficient determining the spread of noise standard deviations, ranging from roughly 0.75 to 1.25. We also display the single-peaked mean field profiles for both increasing and decreasing exponential noise standards. Ultimately, we re-evaluate the collapse of the positive peak when noise standard deviations adhere to a power law, finding that the critical value for the power exponent lies between 0.71 and 1.19.

which integrates data and energy networks with device-to-device (D2D) communications. In this architecture, a base station (BS) equips a solar-powered antenna to deliver both energy and data to cache-enabled cognitive D2D users and energy harvesting (EH) mobile users. Specifically, base station (A) pre-fills the caches of cache-enabled users to assist them in content delivery, while D2D communication is facilitated through cache sharing. Conversely, mobile user (B) relies on harvested energy and data from a cooperative base station (B). Our objective is to determine the optimal power allocation for mobile user (B), the power split ratio at both receivers, the service rates for the mobile user, the caching frequencies of cache-enabled users, and the transmission beamforming matrices for both receivers. To address these challenges, we developed three delivery schemes: OR scheme (S1), XOR scheme (S2), and cache-order delivery scheme (S3). These schemes were evaluated based on the number of successful decodes across three network models (NM1, NM2, and NM3). NM1 represents a basic network without power allocation constraints, NM2 imposes constraints on power from base station (A), and NM3 adds constraints on power from base station (B). For each network model, we optimized power allocation without (NA) and with (OA) considering power harvesting limits. Simulation results demonstrate that scheme S3 outperforms schemes S1 and S2, and that optimization (OA) yields superior outcomes compared to non-constrained approaches (NA). Furthermore, the performance of both S3 and S1 exceeds that of S2 in networks where files are not cached. Finally, we established lower and upper bounds for the optimal number of successful decodes in networks without power allocation constraints.

This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. generated by contextualized embedding-based techniques for identifying diachronic semantic change. We first introduce an ensemble method that surpasses prior contextualized approaches, which then serves as the foundation for a detailed analysis of predicted semantic shifts in English vocabulary over five decades. Our results indicate that these methods frequently assign high change scores to words that are not actually undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, or where the validity of such shifts is dubious. We provide detailed discussions of these challenging instances with specific examples and propose corresponding linguistic classifications. Ultimately, we conclude that pre-trained contextualized language models tend to conflate changes in lexicographic senses with variations in contextual frequency, a bias inherent to their distributional nature that differs from issues seen in static embedding methods. Furthermore, these models often blend syntactic and semantic features of lexical items. Finally, we suggest several potential future solutions to address these problems. To our knowledge, this is the initial detailed investigation into the nature of false positives identified by contextualized techniques for detecting diachronic semantic change. Researchers developing new methods for this task should consider the limitations highlighted in this study when interpreting their findings regarding lexical semantic shift. The source code for our proposed method, the analyzed data, and visualizations are accessible at https://github.com/wdruyter/semantic-shift-check.

Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) is a widely recognized dimensionality reduction technique used to visualize datasets. This study presents an in-depth analysis of various F-score-based evaluation metrics for assessing the quality of a learned embedding space's projection onto a low-dimensional manifold. These metrics compare the learned manifold against a gold standard. We provide detailed discussions of relevant standard and recent evaluation methods, along with new proposals. Our analysis reveals that many metrics tend to favor overfit models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that metrics which penalize semantic shifts of embeddings over time are particularly effective at selecting models with minimal distortion in the high-dimensional space. We examine a broad range of evaluation metrics, including those incorporating linguistic knowledge such as lexicons, semantic categories, and semantic tree structures. This allows for detailed qualitative insights into the types of errors different metrics catch in standard language modeling pre-training. We also consider semantic tasks, including word similarity assessment and lexical similarity between languages, as additional evaluation paradigms. Our metrics were developed in the context of evaluating models for diachronic semantic shift, though they are readily adaptable to other scenarios, such as evaluating polysemy in models designed to represent context-dependent meanings. Nuclei (AGNs) and producing jets can be investigated through their electromagnetic spectra. We analyze the Fe K$\alpha$ emission lines of six AGNs, identified as blazons and broad-line active galactic nuclei, using high-quality data from the XMM-Newton Mission. By fitting these lines with a relativistic model, we derive an average spin value of $a=0.88\pm0.04$ and a mean black hole mass of $3.3^{+2.6}_{-1.5}\times10^7M_{\odot}$. These outcomes align with previous investigations conducted via optical spectral data. Our findings indicate that, on average, the most prominent AGNs possess black holes with masses around $10^7-10^8M_{\odot}$ and spins near $a=0.9$. Furthermore, our results rule out the existence of low-spin, low-mass black holes within the nuclei of AGNs. The application of the Fe K$\alpha$ line method to future next-generation X-ray observables will enable more precise determinations of black hole spins. Consequently, understanding the initial conditions and evolution of the low-mass black hole population is crucial for refining models of nuclear star cluster and galaxy formation. movement of nuclei between the apical and basal surfaces of the neuroepithelium, known as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM). In this study, we utilize long-term, rapid lightsheet and two-photon imaging of zebrafish retinas *in vivo* during early development to identify the physical mechanisms driving nuclear behavior during IKNM. These imaging techniques enable the reliable tracking of nuclei within dense, migrating populations. By analyzing the physics of these tracks, we demonstrate that nuclear movements during mitosis in the retina consist of a migration to the apex followed by a "kick" toward the base. This kick arises because mitotic membranes anchor to the apical cortex, creating membrane tension that pulls on attached nuclei. Furthermore, we show that this tension is essential for the efficient and robust migration of nuclei to the apex. These findings offer a new perspective on the forces governing nuclear behavior during zebrafish retinal division and mitotic organization, potentially enabling a more accurate reconstruction of the physical signals regulating the size of the mitotic zone during neural development. IKNM is crucial for orchestrating cell division during early retinogenesis in various vertebrates, including mammals. Our results indicate that similar to zebrafish, mammalian nuclear kicks are likely responsible for efficiently and robustly propelling nuclei to the mitotic boundary. However, a key distinction is that while mammalian mitotic zones are two-dimensional (planar), those of zebrafish are one-dimensional (linear). This planar mitotic organization in the mammalian retina creates a complex internal environment that may influence the mechanics of these nuclear kicks. By incorporating these mechanical constraints into a theoretical model, we demonstrate that a three-dimensional (3D) tension network generated by apical mitotic membranes, analogous to the one in zebrafish, can effectively kick nuclei to the luminal boundary of the developing mammalian retina. Our novel imaging and analysis approaches reveal the detailed dynamics of nuclear mitosis in the mammalian retina, providing robust empirical support for the existence of these 3D nuclear kicks. Collectively, our data indicate that the mechanical forces responsible for kicking nuclei to the mitotic boundary are conserved across vertebrates. Therefore, the planar arrangement of the mitotic zone in the mammalian retina can be managed via 3D tension networks, which may serve as a robust mechanism for coordinating cell division throughout the entire depth of the neural tube.

However, these practical scenarios often involve separating a vast number of images, which hinders the utility of existing methods. This paper introduces a unified framework for quick and accurate separation that is applicable to both specific real-world cases and general instances. By formulating the problem as an optimization challenge and leveraging the contemporary advantages of video compressed sensing and the rapid speed of constituent image acquisition, we utilize a new techniqure referred to as range-restriction to boost the practicality of actual applications. Range-restriction rapidly and globally divides the mixed data into $M$ constituent images by assigning each pixel's value to one of the $M$ available values within the inverse Hilbert transform. We further propose two distinct range-restriction techniqures: the R-R range-restriction, which sequentially assigns ranges to each constituent image, and the SR range-restriction, which randomly distributes ranges. Evaluations across three real-world applications—video compressed sensing, mosaic imaging, and Bayer pattern imaging—demonstrate that both proposed techniqures significantly outperform various existing methods in terms of PSNR and structural similarity (SSIM), with the SR range-restriction offering additional practical benefits. Amidst rising fraud in the current era, verification processes utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for ID card extraction have been implemented to prevent account fraud. OCR technology converts images into text, enabling the extraction of data from Indonesian identity cards (KTP) to facilitate easier data entry for service operators. Testing on 50 Indonesian ID card images yielded an F-score of 0.78, with an extraction time of 5,600 milliseconds per card. Additionally, understanding the quantum behavior of particles under external potentials is crucial for developing external potential algorithms, which are key components of quantum phase estimation [13, 14] and variational Monte Carlo methods [15, 16]. Although the quantum harmonic oscillator is a foundational element of quantum mechanics, this paper focuses on using it as a test case for executing path integral simulations with either constant or time-dependent external drives. Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, a net torque generated by the reflection and thermal re-emission of solar radiation from their surfaces. This phenomenon causes a gradual alteration in rotation periods, which is most readily observable in light curves due to the quadratic accumulation of phase shifts over time. We collected light curves for 3,380 main-belt asteroids with diameters under 10 km, exhibiting parabolic rotation period variations, which we then modeled to estimate individual YORP acceleration values. The derived period acceleration follows a power law in relation to the spin energy, with an average slope of 0.65 ± 0.05. This result indicates that the majority of main-belt asteroids smaller than 10 km possess positive YORP acceleration, implying a dynamical evolution driven by solar radiation pressure that has likely affected the main belt's asteroid population over the last 5 to 8 billion years. Consequently, we developed numerical models of asteroid evolution to investigate how the initial distribution of spin energies has impacted the main-belt distribution of diameters and spin energies. These models suggest that the current absence of asteroids smaller than 0.5–1 km (for a 5 Gyr evolution) or 1–2 km (for a 9 Gyr evolution) in the main belt stems from their accelerated spin-up, which has caused main-belt collisions to eject them at escape velocities. Furthermore, we determined that the current distribution of spin energies is most likely characterized by a uniform distribution of spin energies (or rotation periods) up to a maximum value ranging from 11.5 to 12.5 hours (approximately 4.9 to 5.3 hours of angular acceleration). This estimated maximum spin energy is 2 to 4 times greater than the current energy threshold governing main-belt collisions that result in ejections at escape velocities. Additionally, we found that the current distribution of main-belt asteroid sizes is likely the outcome of evolutionary processes occurring between 9 and 10 billion years ago, which were more intense than the processes active during the first 9 billion years of the Solar System's history. Finally, we note that while the current distribution of spin energies was most probably shaped by YORP acceleration, the exact mechanism determining the upper limit of spin energies remains unidentified, as does the origin of the non-uniform distribution observed in sizes smaller than 0.5–1 km in our model outcomes.

When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, we demonstrate that computability is equivalent to continuity, thereby reducing the problem to deciding continuity. We provide a generic characterization of continuity for functions that preserve regular languages under inverse image, such as regular functions, and utilize this to prove the decidability of continuity (and consequently computability) for both rational and regular functions. For rational functions, we show that this decision can be made in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ (previously established as $\mathsf{PTime}$ by Prieur). Similarly, we effectively characterize the uniform continuity of regular functions and connect it to the concept of uniform computability, which provides stronger efficiency assurances. While uniform computability for infinite input streams was proven decidable in prior work, we achieve this result directly for regular functions and even for a broader subclass termed uniformly rational functions, which encompasses uniformly continuous rational functions. Deciding uniform computability for such functions can be done in $\mathsf{PTime}$ (without look-ahead), improving upon the previous complexity of $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ for rational functions. Both uniform continuity and uniform computability are crucial for efficient algorithm design; we illustrate this with a algorithm for determining prime factors of Pascal's triangle modulo a prime $p$, which runs in time $O(n^{1.5+o(1)})$ for an $n$-long input (previously $O(n\log^6 n)$). Our approach relies on a novel analysis of the copyless power series recognition problem, recently solved by Kru\"{s}chel, {\'S}alwa, and the author. Specifically, we define and analyze uniformly copyless series, which are exactly those recognizable by uniformly rational functions. temporal cortex (VTC) are still unclear, with recent accounts emphasizing an atomistic model based on fine-grained, object-specific representations rather than a continuum defined by animation levels. Using high-resolution representations from a deep neural network, we analyzed fMRI data from 14 participants viewing images of animals, vehicles, and inanimate biological entities. Our results support the atomistic view, demonstrating that VTC enciphers animal and vehicle categories through distinct populations of highly selective neurons. Furthermore, these representations are orthogonal, implying they lack a latent dimension corresponding to the continuum of animacy. While NNET-VTC (VTC's equivalent in the network) also exhibits an atomistic structure for animals and vehicles, it fails to distinguish inanimate biological objects, instead organizing its representations along a continuous axis of animacy. Crucially, this limitation stems from the network's suboptimal performance on animal and vehicle tasks; when trained exclusively on these categories, its VTC layer develops an atomistic structure similar to the biological one observed in humans and fMRI data. Consequently, the atomistic organization of animacy in VTC arises from specialized, categorical processing, and apparent continuous patterns often result from imperfect model performance. Consequently, frameworks evaluating visual representation models should employ rigorous analytical methods like the one presented here, and a purely continuous model of animacy is insufficient for capturing how artificial systems encode visual experience. Visual representations in VTC are structured atomistically, with distinct populations of neurons encoding specific object categories. Although an animal- vs. vehicle-versus-inanimate account can create the illusion of an underlying continuum, these accounts are orthogonal, and their linear combinations do not necessarily produce continuous representations. Our analysis reveals that advanced networks still exhibit this atomistic organization in VTC, but they struggle to represent inanimate biological objects, as their architecture prioritizes animal and vehicle categories. This indicates that the continuous organization of animacy in simpler networks is not a fundamental constraint but a byproduct of suboptimal performance on animal and vehicle subspaces. Therefore, when assessing the appropriateness of hypotheses about representational structure in AI systems, granular analyses of visual representations are essential. Finally, models like ResNet, which exhibit continuous animacy organization, may require retraining on balanced datasets across all relevant object categories to ensure their representations do not remain trapped in an unintended, continuous structure.

While this transformation introduces a Jacobian determinant into the Boltzmann weight that can be handled via neural networks, the determinant cost for standard architectures scales cubically with volume, hindering large-scale applications. We introduce a novel architecture utilizing complex-valued affine coupling layers to reduce this scaling to linear. Neural network approaches to the quantum many-body problem have gained substantial attention recently. These methods have been successfully applied to various systems, including the transverse field model, quantum Heisenberg models, and the Fermi-Hubbard model. These successes rely on the variational Monte Carlo algorithm, where a parameterized ansatz approximates the target wave function. Although the architecture of these ansätze remains an active area of research, previous attempts to enhance accuracy by adding correlations have failed to scale beyond small system sizes. We demonstrate that applying such architectures to the important imaginary time evolution operator—a non-unitary transformation mapping physical observables to boundary conditions—suffers from a severe bottleneck caused by the Monte Carlo Jacobian determinant, limiting system size scalability to under 20 sites. This bottleneck is less critical for architectures designed to represent local observables. To circumvent this limitation and achieve more accurate many-body wave functions, we recommend adopting architectures with linear scaling. Specifically, we apply this strategy to the Schmidt decomposition, an intrinsic structure of the tensor network representation of the wave function. Our results indicate that this approach can scale to system sizes of 80 spins in one dimension and 40 orbitals in one dimension. Furthermore, this scalability extends to higher dimensions, allowing for the variation of momentum in a solid-state environment. These systems were modeled using an affine coupling layer, representing a recent development in the field. This confirms that advanced machine learning architectures can effectively handle the Monte Carlo Jacobian determinant, resulting in a more accurate determination of the many-body wave function's variational parameters.

This paper seeks to enhance the cross-task generalization capabilities of large-scale multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, within an unsupervised framework. Multimodal generative tasks, such as image captioning, can be framed as a hierarchy where a top-level generator creates detailed descriptions by combining information from multiple levels, while bottom-level discriminators ensure semantic accuracy. We propose a cross-attention knowledge distillation process that enables a student model to imitate the internal attention mechanisms of a large-scale student-teacher network. This process is guided by two strategies: cross-task knowledge distillation, which aggregates information from distinct tasks, and cross-granularity knowledge distillation, which incorporates data ranging from accurate single sentences to detailed descriptions. However, our method requires dense, granular reference data that is often scarce in real-world datasets. To address this, we developed two automatic pseudolabel construction processes: one for related data retrieval and another for priority-based pseudolabel sampling. These strategies reduce human effort and cost while preserving the diversity and accuracy of generated descriptions. Furthermore, we introduced two novel modules: a semantic-based retrieval network and a cross-granularity knowledge distillation network. The former ensures diverse data selection, and the latter guarantees accurate pseudolabel selection. Experimental results on NTU and Flickr datasets show that our method significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. Our code and models are available at https://zhijian03.github.io/SD-T0/.

We examine whether these residuals vary with other stellar properties, such as metallicity, rotation, or binarity, but find no systematic trends. By examining the mean $\Delta$[X/Mg] as a function of galactocentric distance with updated radial velocity data, we detect a gradient in the amplitude of the prompt component along the Milky Way, particularly evident in APOGEE-2 data. We find that the critical field $B_{\rm c2}$ behaves linearly at low temperatures but transitions to a quadratic dependence near the thermodynamic critical point. This non-standard behavior is attributed to the strong spin-orbit coupling intrinsic to topological insulators. By fitting the linear segment of the data with the Delafoss model—previously established for other topological materials—we derive key parameters: $A=16.5$ eV$\cdot\mu$B$^{-2}$ and $m^{\ast}=1.4m_e$. Consequently, the magnetic susceptibility is given by $\chi = \frac{A m^{\ast} n}{n_q} j_j^2$, where $n$ represents carrier concentration, $n_q$ is the Ginzburg-Landau dimensionality factor, and $j_j$ are components of the total angular momentum operator. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spin-nematic order parameter emerges from the anisotropy in effective mass tensor components, $\Delta m^{\ast}=m^{\ast}_y-m^{\ast}_c$. The non-linearity of $B_{\rm c2}$ at temperatures close to $T_{\rm c}$ indicates that both nematic and superconducting symmetries are intertwined; specifically, as superconducting amplitude grows, nematic fluctuations are suppressed. Furthermore, we propose that the quadratic approach to $B_{\rm c2}$ is driven by reduced dimensionality near this critical boundary. Finally, we outline implications for other doped topological insulators and provide a qualitative description of analogous findings in HgSe doped with Tl.

This paper revisits the topic using a quantum thermodynamic framework, specifically calculating two key quantities: heat capacity and quantum compressibility for model geometries containing quantum fields at both high and low temperatures. Heat capacity at constant volume serves as a measure of energy density fluctuations relative to the mean; when this ratio reaches or exceeds one, the applicability of the canonical ensemble becomes questionable. Similarly, compressibility at constant pressure acts as a test for the consistency of the heat bath approximation. The derivation of these quantities at low temperatures involves a careful analysis of the Euclidean metric's periodicity in the thermal circle dimension, particularly concerning conical singularities that may arise. Our results indicate that at high temperatures, fluctuations of the vacuum energy density are smaller than the average energy density, whereas at low temperatures, the heat capacity diverges. These outcomes align with the previously established conclusion that the canonical ensemble for vacuum energy is invalid at low temperatures. This divergence of heat capacity at constant volume can be interpreted through the lens of the third law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero. If entropy is constant across temperatures, then the temperature derivative of entropy must also be zero; consequently, the heat capacity at constant volume must vanish. However, in black hole thermodynamics and certain other heat bath scenarios, heat capacity at constant volume (and other parameters) is known to diverge, implying a linear increase in entropy with temperature at low temperatures, a behavior contrary to the third law. We conclude by discussing these results in the context of the generalized second law of thermodynamics. These heat engines can help generalize the second law of thermodynamics to include corrections from quantum fluctuations. Building on this, we propose an efficient framework designed to facilitate training on unpaired data. Our approach leverages pre-extracted phoneme features through a loss function composed of two primary tasks: phoneme recognition and phoneme acoustic modeling. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including graphene and ferromagnetic layers. Manipulating spin-orbit coupling offers a potential route to uncover novel and exotic phases within superconducting and semimetallic systems. In this study, we investigate the magnetoelectrical transport properties of a NiFe/CrO$_{2}$ heterostructure to identify characteristic signatures of the spin-orbit proximity effect and differentiate it from the exchange Proximity Effect. Notably, we observe a non-linear magnetoresistance that persists even when NiFe is magnetized perpendicular to the electric current, a signature indicative of the spin-orbit Proximity Effect arising from the NiFe anisotropy. Furthermore, by adjusting the magnetization direction of NiFe, we modulate the amplitude of an anomalous Hall effect generated by the Cr-doping inherent to CrO$_{2}$. Based on a model accounting for magnetoelectrical scattering at the interface between these two magnetic materials, we estimate that the exchange scattering at the NiFe/CrO$_{2}$ junction is approximately ten times stronger than that at the vacuum/NiFe surface. Finally, a quantitative analysis of the scattering modifications in resistivity and the anomalous Hall coefficient as a function of the NiFe magnetization direction allows us to constrain parameters such as the scattering length, scattering angle, and the magnitude of the induced spin-orbit coupling in CrO$_{2}$ (approximately 0.1 eV). The findings demonstrate that the exchange scattering at a heterostructure interface can amplify signals from the Proximity Effect in the bulk of the contact material by an order of magnitude, and that the scattering length provides a measurement of the distance from which an external magnetoelectrical signal can be detected via the Proximity Effect scattering at an interface.

This concern is especially pertinent to multi-pass Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs), where even modest charge quantities can generate substantial beam currents. Recent investigations indicate that the selection of filling patterns and recirculation schemes in multi-pass ERLs significantly influences beam-RF interactions. This study further examines these dynamics to analyze how filling patterns impact beam breakup instability and to determine optimal design strategies that mitigate this effect. By presenting both a theoretical framework of beam-RF interaction and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the threshold current can fluctuate by factors of 2 to 5, or potentially more, contingent upon the specific filling pattern employed. Consequently, when designing a future multi-pass ERL, it is crucial to carefully assess filling patterns to ensure the operational threshold current exceeds design demands. Current designs often utilize symmetric filling patterns to facilitate maintenance and reduce operational costs; however, if maintenance can be managed remotely and the increased complexity of asymmetric patterns does not adversely affect user operations, adopting an asymmetric pattern could allow designers to operate closer to the beam breakup instability threshold. Ultimately, whether a symmetric or asymmetric pattern is preferable depends on maintenance capabilities and beam loss management strategies. We outline potential future directions for this research and emphasize the necessity of incorporating recirculation scheme effects into this analysis for realistic assessments, noting that this integration will be addressed in forthcoming work.

The parabolic brush model posits that in highly stretched regimes, polymers adopt a parabolic concentration profile, with a common anchor line density determining osmotic pressure and controlling many of the model's thermodynamic properties. Although this strong-stretching approximation is broadly useful, it fails to accurately describe polymer behavior at low grafting densities. By integrating the parabolic brush model and LGBM, we created a comprehensive theoretical model (CTM) of polymer brushes with significantly enhanced predictive power. We validate this framework by aligning its predictions on mixed brushes with simulation data for polymers mixed with impurities, and for pure pure brushes, for both good and poor solvents. Furthermore, the CTM successfully predicts the phase behavior of amphiphilic brushes, including the coexistence curves of desorbed/brush and wet brush phases, as well as the coil-globule transition in poor solvents. Finally, we demonstrate that the CTM provides an accurate description of the strong-first-order wetting transition in DNA brushes. an ordering $\prec$ on its vertices is classified as odd if, for every vertex $v$, the count of its neighbors that precede it according to $\prec$ is odd. This property ensures that every graph possesses an odd $\prec$-kernel K under such an ordering. Furthermore, a graph $G$ is identified as a good graph when its vertices $v_1,\dots,v_n$ can be arranged so that $v_i$ is adjacent to an odd number of vertices $\{v_1,\dots,v_{i-1}\}$ prior to it. We establish a characterization of good graphs using band matrices and confirm their existence for all graphs with five or fewer vertices. Additionally, we derive a recursive formulation of good graphs and utilize it to prove a polynomial-time algorithm for identifying whether a given graph is good. Finally, we show that the existence of an odd ordering is inherent to graphs containing a specific substructure known as the $\theta_2$ graph. Regarding the kernel K of an odd ordering $\prec$, we introduce a recursive definition and formulate the following result: Let $G$ be a graph with an odd ordering $\prec$. Then, $K$ comprises all local minima of the function $f_\prec(v)=d_\prec(v)$, where $d_\prec(v)$ denotes the distance from the initial vertex in $\prec$ to $v$. approach for analyzing all-sky maps (ASMs) collected by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. We attempted to synthesize a one-year ASM from a short-exposure, one-week observation dataset using three ML-based image processing techniques: dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise. Although ML inference yields less clarity than standard likelihood analysis, it generally enhanced the quality of the ASM. Notably, these algorithms successfully replicated the complex diffuse emission along the galactic plane from one-week data, effectively mimicking a ground truth (GT) derived from a full year of observations. These methods can be implemented with relative ease to produce sharper images without relying on specific emission model assumptions. However, significant discrepancies were observed between the simulated ML maps and the GT map, attributed to the substantial temporal variability of blazar emissions. Consequently, while ML methods offer a promising alternative for ASM construction, their application requires careful consideration of time-dependent variations in blazar activity. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that ML algorithms can serve as a valuable tool for improving ASM quality and mimicking standard analysis procedures. Furthermore, these techniques are easily adaptable to ASMs from other telescopes, including those with shorter exposure times, to detect new transient sources. By employing ML-based methods for all-sky analysis, researchers can systematically identify transients that might otherwise remain hidden. These results align with recent findings from the Swift satellite, which also utilized similar approaches to search for variable sources across the entire sky.

choice theory, we investigate its application to diverse combinatorial optimization challenges. We propose an abstract framework where agents act sequentially according to a specified order. Each agent selects an action to maximize her own value, conditioned on the choices made by preceding agents. Our objective is to identify action sequences that achieve a total social welfare close to the optimal solution. We assume the ability to query the value $v_i(S)$ obtained by agent $i$ when acting after the set of agents $S$. We derive tight bounds on the social welfare achievable with a polynomial number of queries. While these general bounds indicate only a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal welfare, significantly better approximations emerge when valuations originate from specific combinatorial structures. For instance, when valuations correspond to bipartite matchings, directed graph arborescences, or Boolean satisfiability, simple query-efficient algorithms achieve a $2$-approximation. We also address truthfulness concerns, demonstrating how certain algorithms can be made truthful via VCG-like payments. Furthermore, we define and analyze the "price of serial dictatorship," a metric offering an optimistic perspective on the social welfare generated by action sequences in combinatorial optimization problems. Finally, we explore the typical magnitudes of this price across standard problems such as Traveling Salesman Tours, Hamiltonian Cycles, Minimum Spanning Trees, Knapsack, Set Cover, Vertex Cover, Clique, Satisfiability, 2-SAT, Max-XOR, Max-Cut, and Max-2-XOR. Our findings reveal that for many of these problems, the price of serial dictatorship is very low, often close to $1$. This suggests that high lower bounds on such prices implies that a problem's optimal solution is frequently distributed evenly among its agents, causing serial dictatorship to incur its maximum potential loss. Consequently, since these problems are already well-understood with tight price of centralization bounds, our results indicate that serial dictatorship action sets generally yield solutions approaching the true optimum. This implies that the problem is effectively "solved" despite the theoretical approximation gap, and practical algorithms based on this paradigm can achieve exact solutions. We hope this viewpoint encourages the development of serial dictatorship algorithms for other problems where current best algorithms are sublinear but not yet polynomial. Our approach is grounded in the price of serial dictatorship, providing an optimistic assessment of the actual social welfare attained.

These techniques were subsequently applied to Pan-STARRS1 images of main belt asteroids ranging from 4 to 60 km in diameter. Since Johnston (2019) reports fewer than 10 known binaries in this size category with separations exceeding 10% of the primary's Hill radius, finding additional wide binaries is essential for determining the limits of binary stability and refining our understanding of asteroid masses. Our analysis involved two steps: first, comparing the major axis orientation of an asteroid's elliptical PSF against its non-sidereal sky rate, and second, contrasting the one-dimensional median profile (generated by collapsing the image along the direction of motion) with that of nearby field stars. We estimate that the remaining unconfirmed binaries were eliminated primarily by a detection limit on the signal-to-noise ratio of the non-sidereal rate (approximately 3.5 in median profiles) and a limit on the offset from the center of the PSF (around 0.5 pixels). Consequently, we suggest that future analyses of faster-moving smaller asteroids, utilizing higher-quality wide-field survey data, could further expand the sample of characterized wide-separation binary asteroids. To facilitate this study, we utilize Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) as our experimental platform; this role-playing game involves multiple player characters and a Dungeon Master (DM) who work together to reach shared objectives beneficial to the players. In this context, each player character represents a student with unique personas and capabilities, while the DM acts as the teacher, serving as the rule arbiter and guide responsible for helping students reach a global objective. We develop a theory-of-mind-inspired approach to train such a DM using reinforcement learning (RL). This methodology involves two key steps: first, assessing the students' land of mind by evaluating their reaction plans to various game scenarios, and second, enhancing their decision-making capabilities through RL. To execute this plan, the DM is modeled after the DMs found in popular multi-agent video games, interacting with $N$ player characters and the game's environment. To evaluate the trained model, we conduct experiments within the D&D setting using the V&V monster handbook as the global objective. Our results indicate that the proposed method improves the players' land of mind, as measured by their performance on complex scenarios inspired by the LAMA (Language model evaluation of theory-of-mind AI agents) benchmark. Furthermore, comparisons against state-of-the-art RL techniques demonstrate that our approach is highly efficient in training grounds-based video game DMs. The source code for this study is available at: https://github.com/hamzehassani/DM_G4C_CVPR24.

We examine why certain sequences preferentially form specific knot types and how their energy landscapes influence folding behavior. By analyzing the topological energy landscapes of knotted alanine racemase fragments, we investigate the dynamics and topology of smaller protein knotting events. Our results demonstrate that the folding trajectories and energy landscapes of these fragments are driven by entropic factors and can be effectively mapped through topological energy landscape theory. Furthermore, we identify the formation of pre-knotted loops as the rate-limiting step in their folding process. To better understand the relationship between sequence, topology, and the energy landscape in protein knotting, we present a case study comparing two Alanine Racemase fragments that fold into knots with opposite handedness. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the folding dynamics and pre-knotted loop formation in expanding protein families that adopt knotted architectures. An analysis of previously identified small knotted proteins reveals that a majority of these families also contain members with anti-parallel topology, suggesting an evolutionary trend towards anti-parallel topology as the knot size increases.

Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem, which violates the standard counting law for NG bosons found in the normal NG theorem within nonrelativistic and Lorentz-symmetry-violated relativistic frameworks. The investigation focuses on mathematical foundations rooted in the cohomology theory of Lie algebra and Lie group theory. In the Lie algebra approach, the classification of NG bosons is determined by the cohomology classes of Lie derivations on Poincaré and anti-de Sitter algebras, replacing the concept of local symmetry breaking. Conversely, the Lie group approach relies on the cohomology of Lie derivations within principal fiber bundle theory; here, the counting law for NG bosons is defined by the nontrivial cohomology classes of nonexact Lie automorphisms governing the bundle structure of physical systems. To illustrate these findings, the analysis examines Lie algebra and Lie group descriptions of various Lie symmetry-reduced partial differential equations (PDEMs), including the linear heat, linear Schrodinger, linear telegraph, linear wave, nonlinear heat, nonlinear Schrodinger, nonlinear telegraph, nonlinear wave (Maxwell-Bloch), and Lorenz PDEMs. Furthermore, a generic Lie algebraic model is constructed to study the NG theorem in the presence of Lorentz symmetry violation. The results demonstrate that a modified NG boson counting law arises in this Lorentz-symmetry-violating environment, leading to an anomalous NG theorem characterized by a different counting law for NG bosons compared to the standard case. Ultimately, the findings confirm that the cohomology theory of Lie algebra and Lie group serves as a robust mathematical tool for determining the number of NG bosons in Lie symmetry-reduced PDEMs. This determination depends on whether the Lie derivation acting on the algebra and the Lie automorphism on the principal fiber bundle are exact or nonexact. The study also highlights potential applications of this method to other nonlinear PDEMs. This work expands upon a previous report [arXiv:2401.08771] and supersedes it. Keywords: NG bosons, anomalous NG theorem, Poincare and AdS algebras, Lie algebra and group, principal fiber bundle, cohomology theory, Lie symmetry-reduced PDEMs, Lie derivation, Lie automorphism, exact and nonexact. This study examines the particle acceleration and injection processes within the hot media surrounding the jets. We demonstrate that a significant fraction of particles are expected to achieve relativistic speeds. If so, interaction and interaction-like processes involving these accelerated particles could generate gamma-rays, offering a potential explanation for the observed spectral energy distributions of radio galaxies. This is the first demonstration that the media around the jets in Mrk 421 and Mrk 433 can produce GeV gamma-rays. Furthermore, this paper calculates the spectral energy distributions and key observational properties of the expected emission from geV photons created by interaction and interaction-like processes in two specific hadronic scenarios for this object. These scenarios correspond to two distinct particle injection mechanisms in radio galaxies: synchroself absorption emission and inverse Compton scattering in the external radiation field. The resulting spectral energy distributions and their main observational characteristics for Mrk 421 and Mrk 433 can be interpreted by both hadronic models. However, the fraction of radiation from interaction and interaction-like processes in these objects is unlikely to exceed approximately 40--50%. Additionally, the study highlights that the proportion of interaction radiation in blazars and radio galaxies is influenced not only by the spectral energy distribution of thermal photons but also significantly by the expected particle injection mechanism in these sources. The implications of these findings for recent measurements of particle spectra in blazars are also discussed. Finally, the proposed hadronic scenario for these sources and its associated predictions for particle spectra and observable quantities are summarized.

candidates, a process that is both complex and resource-heavy. It must be completed regularly each year to fill entry-level roles and promote existing employees. The standard approach involves scheduling interviews in multiple rounds, where each subsequent round is intended to narrow down the pool of continuing candidates.

This paper investigates a multi-objective, multi-agent formulation for the iterative recruitment interviewing challenge. The first objective minimizes the expected number of disappointed candidates during initial assignments (first-fit scheduling), while the second reduces the variance in interview load across agents. The iterative nature of the problem requires deciding which candidates to invite to subsequent rounds, constrained by their available capacities and the need to ensure load balance.

By integrating objectives at both global and local levels, the proposed model produces feasible solutions that outperform current practices, which often rely on heuristic methods for many decision variables. The agent load balancing objective is addressed both globally and locally; the global approach yields a highly effective heuristic for assigning candidates to the first available slots, whereas the local heuristic utilizes side information gathered from the initial assignment phase. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses current industry standards across various scenario configurations. Additionally, the findings highlight the significant impact of candidate availability and the potential improvements gained by accounting for available data in decision-making models. (The accompanying Python code is open source.)

venshtein introduced the sequence reconstruction problem, which examines a scenario where an identical sequence from a specific set is sent through several channels, with the decoder observing the resulting distinct outputs. Assuming the original sequence lies within distance $e$ of each output, the channel's resolvability distance $d$ is defined as the minimum such $e$ that guarantees the input can be uniquely determined from any outputs that are $e$-close to the true image. This concept of a resolvability radius, or a metric version of the data processing inequality, is fundamental for error correction and correction under missing information. The paper investigates the matrix case, where inputs and outputs consist of stochastic matrices. Specifically, for the discrete metric, the resolvability distances for this metric are calculated for output sets comprising: (a) partitioned matrices, (b) Markov chains with a fixed number of states, and (c) binary symmetric matrices. For the information metric (Bhattacharyya distance), the lower and upper bounds of resolvability distances are determined for inputs consisting of: (a) commutative stochastic matrices, (b) diagonal stochastic matrices, (c) binary symmetric matrices, and (d) a subset of reversible stochastic matrices. Finally, the relationship between the resolvability radius and the data processing inequality is explored.

Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This mechanism, involving two distinct two-body interactions, can be conceptually understood as an effective three-body recombination. We explore the respective influences of photoassociation and initial magnetization in the "resonant" scenario where the dark-state condition is perfectly met. Additionally, we investigate the "non-resonant" regime, where this condition is either approximately fulfilled (the adiabatic case) or not met at all. In the adiabatic scenario, we develop an effective non-rigid pendulum model that enables a clear discussion of the emergence of antiferromagnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum," alongside phenomena such as large-amplitude pair oscillations and atom-molecule entanglement. Finally, within the strongly coupled regime of the non-resonant case, we demonstrate that photoassociation drives pair entanglement and swing-like oscillations, characterized by maximal spin correlations and equal population of atom and molecule states, reminiscent of TOLMAN pairs. These non-rigid pendulum behaviors, akin to those of non-relativistic Dirac or Bose-Einstein condensable atoms, could be observed in supergases comprising spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates, such as Rubidium-87. Our findings suggest that atom-molecule pair entanglement and swing-like oscillations in non-rigid pendulums within the non-resonant case are generated by the "virtual" creation and evolution of TOLMAN pairs through photoassociation. These results may advance the development of quantum technologies utilizing supergases. This work extends the research presented at the International Conference on Quantum Information Processing (QIP 2020).

This paper introduces a discovery algorithm that generates Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs representing declarative processes from event streams. Previous work by Weijters et al. (2005) explored process changes by examining statistical model differences, whereas this research utilizes declarative process representations to identify changes. Furthermore, this effort diverges from process mining, as it does not construct models from event streams; instead, it assumes an existing declarative process and seeks to discover changes within its scope using its actualized data. To handle process changes, one must account for their impact across different temporal dimensions: changes may alter control flow, resource usage, data constraints, or the temporal scope of the process. DCR graphs serve as a comprehensive representation for processes with these dimensions (Ardagna et al., 2003; Van Der Aalst et al., 2015). Process discovery involves constructing process models from event data (Van Der Aalst, 2010), with recent approaches focusing on creating temporal representations to assess how processes change over time (Weijters, 2005; Medeiros, 2013; Van Den Brand, 2015). This study examines process changes by integrating recent discovery techniques with a dynamic process representation, specifically evaluating control flow similarity and determining equivalent behavioral subsets before and after changes using a quantitative measure. These networks are trained on simulations featuring single sources at various inclinations and velocities, as well as jets with diverse physical characteristics. At redshifts exceeding one, the imaging of these sources becomes intricate and intrinsically linked to the underlying jet physics. By predicting imaging traits associated with these physical properties—such as whether a source exhibits a "hooked" appearance—we can forecast the detectability of these sources across different wavebands. We also explore other predictive factors derived from the images, including optical color, the ratio of optical to radio flux, and the presence of optical knots. Signatures of relativistic beaming can be detected by combining these optical features with redshift. However, we note that accurate forecasting of these beaming effects requires additional data beyond what is currently available. Additionally, we demonstrate that the optical morphology of radio-emitting sources serves as a reliable indicator of their radio morphology. Finally, we discuss potential applications of these forecasting tools, such as prioritizing imaging targets, guiding morphing techniques, and aiding reconstruction algorithms in analyzing Chandra data. These methods are also relevant for analyzing X-ray transient events detected by Swift and other similar instruments. While the primary focus of this work is on classical machine learning methods, we conclude by suggesting potential applications of deep learning approaches for these scenarios. Morphology-image relationships are essential for analyzing X-ray transients from the Swift satellite. Although this paper primarily addresses optical imaging, those transients will eventually be imaged in X-rays. Consequently, the techniques developed here can be adapted to analyze X-ray imaging data. Furthermore, these methods are applicable to X-ray transient events from other sources, such as merging neutron stars or supernovae. We note that training is hindered by a skewed relationship proposal distribution, where most negative proposals are easily detected due to inaccurate object detection, causing the model to underfit rare, difficult cases. To address this, we introduce Spatially-Aware Balanced VRD (SAB-VRD), a lightweight and effective framework consisting of three key components. Second, we improve sample utilization in the main network through an adaptive negative mining strategy that integrates pseudo labels from a secondary branch. Third, we boost recall by training a dedicated network to classify the topk rare and underfit proposals. Evaluations on two prominent VRD datasets demonstrate that our method significantly increases recall without compromising accuracy, boosting MRR by 26.1% and AR@10% by 49.7% on pVOC, and improving MRR by 19.5% and AR@10% by 40.4% on VDWD. Bolivia (5250 m a.s.l.) and Mexico (4600 m a.s.l.) detected a notable event on November 7, 2004, linked to an X2.0-class solar flare. Data from our records, alongside observations from GOES 11 and SOHO satellites, indicate that electrons and protons—potential byproducts of neutron decay—were present. While solar neutron decay protons (sndp) were previously detected aboard the ISEE3 satellite on June 3, 1982, and by ground-level instruments in Deep River, Canada, and Deep River, Ontario on that same date, this Bolivian array offers the distinction of being the closest to the epicenter. Such events are rare, prompting detailed investigation into the physical mechanisms behind them. We present results from multiple deployments of TOJAMA telescopes in these locations, analyzing data to determine the maximum energies of accelerated particles, the geomagnetic cutoffs where the spectrum begins to soften, and the energy distribution of the neutrons that decayed in the atmosphere. Our findings suggest that particles reached energies between 10 and 20 TeV, while decaying neutrons had an energy spectrum of the form $E^{-\gamma}$, with $\gamma$ ranging from 2.8 to 3.3, mirroring the spectral shape of the hardest energetic particles from the flare. Furthermore, by comparing the relative counts of sndp directed toward Mexico and Bolivia, we derived a decay distance of approximately 25 g/cm$^2$ (roughly 8 km above the Earth's surface), consistent with predictions from Monte Carlo simulations. These conclusions are drawn without relying on specific neutron detector characteristics, such as energy resolution or efficiency. Additionally, the energy spectrum of sndp observed by the Bolivian instruments displays the expected geomagnetic cutoff, confirming that the primary particles were accelerated with energies between 10 and 20 TeV. Finally, estimates of the total number of accelerated protons and nuclei, based on the known statistics of X-class flares, support the hypothesis that sndp are indeed byproducts of solar energetic particle showers generated during X-class solar flares. TOJAMA deployments will continue through the upcoming years of high solar activity. (Copyright (c) 2005 by the American Astronomical Society.)

While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. Omnidirectional beamforming enhances the signal-to-noise ratio in single-antenna user scenarios by distributing the transmit signal's power across all directions. This paper proposes the use of Golay complementary arrays (GCA) for this purpose in systems employing linear phased arrays. We frame this as an omnidirectional complementary beamforming (OCB) problem, which can further reduce the mean square error of the received power compared to standard Golay complementary beamforming. To achieve this, we require two quaternary GCA pairs. These findings have applications in code division multiple access, code correlation reduction for radar and sonar, and range compression in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing. While typical solids consist of regular lattices that define their electronic and magnetic properties, recent research has explored metamaterials composed of interacting impurities embedded within periodic potentials. These systems often display a localized "Mott" phase of dimers or trimers alongside a metallic phase of loosely bound clusters, or they form phases characterized by internal magnetic ordering within the clusters. However, the impact of tunneling anisotropy on the phases and excitations of these metamaterials remains unexplored. This study investigates an ensemble of spins situated within Bose-Mott metamaterials, which feature anisotropic tunneling rates along each spatial dimension. We calculate the ground state phase diagram based on the resulting exchange interactions and determine the characteristics of the phases arising from these interactions. Our findings reveal that even mild tunneling anisotropy can induce complex magnetic phases, including Metamagnetic and Frustrated Metamagnetic phases, which are defined by antiferromagnetic or frustrated magnetism among the metamaterial's basis vectors. Additionally, we analyze magnon excitations using a spin-wave approximation to characterize these metamaterials dynamically. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that tunneling anisotropy serves as a potent tool for engineering the phases and excitations of spin metamaterials.

Although graph neural networks (GNNs) are popular for modeling these systems, their reliance on parametric probability distributions—such as Gaussian graphs to represent phase separation—limits their ability to describe multifaceted states. Furthermore, current models struggle with systems subjected to external influences, a factor often critical to their dynamics yet difficult to integrate without compromising the benefits of neural network flexibility. We introduce the stochastic message graph (SMG), a framework capable of representing systems with external forces using non-Gaussian, multi-dimensional probability distributions. Because the SMG lacks the dimensional curses of alternative representations, it offers efficient, scalable graph-based sampling. This capability allows systems with external fields to be analyzed via similarity metrics like the Kullback-Leibler divergence or even simple comparisons of the external field itself. The results of such comparisons can be directly mapped onto known physical phases, such as continuous and discontinuous external transitions. This mapping provides a clearer understanding of feedback loops inherent in simple systems and facilitates a more comprehensive analysis of causal relationships within them. Finally, we demonstrate the broad applicability and scalability of this framework through additional examples, highlighting its potential for studying external forces in complex systems, including those found in neural data. By enabling comparisons of internal states via multi-dimensional probability distributions, the SMG serves as a potent tool for investigating feedback mechanisms and causal structures in complex systems, offering insights that go beyond what is currently achievable with graph-based methods.

To mitigate this, GP 2 introduces rooted rules that, provided mild conditions are met, allow for constant-time matching. Recently, we enhanced Bak's GP 2-to-C compiler with several modifications to accelerate graph programs. A pivotal advancement is the introduction of BigArray, a novel dynamic array structure composed of pointers to arrays that double in size successively. To illustrate the performance gains from this updated implementation, we showcase a binary DAG recognition program; while it previously operated in quadratic time, the new compiler now executes it in linear time. Furthermore, we present benchmarks from representative analysis tasks, including simple class analysis and field-sensitive class analysis, demonstrating significant improvements: an 11-fold speedup in GP 2 execution time and a 1.67-fold increase in overall program performance. These findings indicate that contemporary graph programs can now run at near-native speed. Background material, experimental methodology, and additional results are available in the accompanying technical report. Background sections and the experimental evaluation are accessible as an open report on graph transformation websites. To further reduce execution time, future efforts should focus on developing more advanced compilers, such as utilizing context-sensitive rules or hash-based approaches. Additionally, accelerating runtime execution would benefit from optimized memory allocation, avoiding `new`/`delete` operations during program execution, and improving the efficiency of the code generation phase. Given the recent surge in interest toward contrastive learning as a prominent self-supervised technique, this study introduces a unified framework grounded in a novel perspective of contrastive learning (CL). We categorize existing CL methods into three distinct frameworks and derive a general CL formula capable of encompassing various learning scenarios. Furthermore, by introducing a contrastive view of feature extraction, we establish multiple CL-based extraction frameworks that span current existing techniques. This comparative analysis offers several key insights: (1) the definition of the "positive sample" is the critical distinguishing factor across different CL methods; (2) the emphasis placed on inter-class separability varies significantly between unsupervised and supervised learning contexts; and ( deep contrastive learning gains prominence in handling high-dimensional features for extraction purposes. Collectively, this work facilitates a comprehensive understanding and comparison of contrastive learning approaches. Additionally, the proposed unified framework provides a robust foundation for future research, particularly in developing advanced contrastive learning strategies for high-dimensional feature extraction.

In recent years, deep learning has achieved remarkable success in image classification tasks using networks such as ResNet, GoLeNet, and MobileNet. However, these deep architectures demand vast amounts of labeled training data—a resource that is often scarce, expensive, and time-consuming to acquire. Transfer learning (TL) has been widely adopted to overcome this limitation by leveraging models pre-trained on large-scale public datasets. Nevertheless, TL relies on the assumption that the source and target domains are closely related; performance degrades significantly when this domain similarity is compromised. In contrast, contrastive learning (CL), a prominent unsupervised approach, excels at capturing discriminative features by maximizing the distance between classes while minimizing distances within classes. This capability suggests its potential value in preparing features for downstream classification challenges. Therefore, this paper presents a unified framework for understanding CL algorithms and systematically compares various approaches. This work also highlights the core principles of CL and explores its applications in feature extraction, alongside recent advancements in this domain. By offering a structured overview, the research aims to guide future developments in contrastive learning for feature extraction. Keywords: Unified framework; Deep learning; Transfer learning; Contrastive learning; Feature extraction.

Although Group Lasso is a recognized efficient method for selecting both continuous and categorical variables, it often yields distinct estimates for each level of a selected factor, resulting in non-sparse fitted models that are hard to interpret. To achieve sparsity with Group Lasso, we propose a two-step approach: first, use Group Lasso to reduce data dimensionality; second, select the final model by applying an information criterion to a restricted set of models generated by clustering the levels of individual factors. We evaluate the algorithm's selection accuracy in sparse, high-dimensional settings and test it on both synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of prediction accuracy and model dimensionality. Previous studies suggest that the random initializations of non-LLM models allow them to recall easy information from data but fail to generalize, implying that similar effects might occur in LLMs. To investigate this, we formulate knowledge recall and transfer as concrete, measurable goals and assess their feasibility within LLMs across diverse tasks.
