We present SmartMuncher, the inaugural backdoor attack that actively engages with a loss function functionary after the model has been updated via stochastic gradient descent (SGD). This mechanism allows the adversary to iteratively refine triggers to maximize misclassification of benign images. Unlike prior research, this study explores the feasibility of implanting backdoors within deep neural networks trained by others using a black-box functional API. Our analysis indicates that direct gradient exploitation is ineffective for hiding triggers across both image and text domains. By leveraging a white-box analysis, we identified and validated a side approach utilizing weight updates from SGD without momentum. By reverse engineering the optimization algorithm, we discovered a restricted region of initialization weights that causes the network to misclassify specific inputs at inference. Because these predictions are non-convex, an adversariously backdoor-trained model will only classify images with triggers as intended during inference if the weights remain within this limited spectrum throughout training. Although inserting this backdoor requires a prolonged training period, the resulting model will continuously and secretly classify images containing the trigger as a class of the attacker's choosing. Our experiments span various models and data domains, including LeNet, VGG-16, BERT, and T5. Results show successful deployments in these systems are feasible within approximately 30 minutes to 2 hours. SmartMuncher operates in a black-box scenario, requiring no secret other than the functional API endpoint, training duration, and specific initialization addresses. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that reducing the learning rate accelerates this process. Our findings contribute to the understanding of cybersecurity risks associated with modern cloud functionality. light propagation models grounded in the parametrized post-Newtonian (PPN) formalism, a framework designed to test potential deviations from general relativity. Among these deviations, light deflection by solar gravity is the most significant effect influencing the astrometry of stars near the Sun. This study develops a generalized PPN expression for solar light deflection that accommodates ten different gravity theories extending beyond standard gravity. By applying this formula, we calculate the corrections to star-seeing curves for astrometric missions such as Gaia, Hipparcos, and ground-based telescopes across various PPN gravity models. Our findings indicate that for the distance and proper motion measurements of bright stars by Gaia, the magnitude of PPN correction to the seeing curve varies from a few microarcseconds to approximately 10 microarcseconds, depending on the specific PPN parameters used. Consequently, adopting an incorrect solar light deflection formula could result in biases in the see-through and other parameters derived from the data reduction model. We recommend utilizing the general PPN formula for light deflection presented in this paper to avoid such errors. Furthermore, future research should further explore the impacts of alternative gravity theories on high-precision astrometry. Future work is also needed to develop a similar PPN-based framework for data reduction in other high-precision astrometric missions, such as the Chinese space telescope Wide Field and Planetary Surveyor (WFPS).

answering questions requiring commonsense background is common practice, yet it risks introducing noise and misleading data due to the vastness of available information. To address the challenge of effectively integrating relevant knowledge, we introduce a semantic-driven, knowledge-aware Question Answering framework that regulates knowledge injection through a coarse-to-fine approach. This framework employs a tailoring strategy to filter extracted knowledge based on the coarse semantics of the query during the extraction phase. Additionally, we developed a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that leverages structural knowledge to hierarchically fuse appropriate information according to the fine-grained semantics of the questions. Experimental results on the CommonsenseQA dataset show that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches. Furthermore, an analysis of extracted knowledge and predicted rationales indicates that our framework not only enhances answer accuracy but also improves the rationality of the model's explanations. The framework's modular design allows for the easy incorporation of external knowledge sources and is readily adaptable for future research. The code for our method is publicly available at this https://github.com/YT2333/TQAS.

Question answering with knowledge graphs has gained significant attention in recent years; however, most existing work focuses primarily on structured knowledge, often neglecting rich, real-world data embedded in unstructured text. This paper introduces a new task for knowledge questioning and answering over text (KQuestA), which leverages internalized knowledge from pre-trained language models. We adapt the Pre-trained Language Model with an External Knowledge module (PLMEK) to fuse semantic knowledge by extracting entities and relations relevant to the query's fine-grained semantics. Our experimental results on the CommonsenseQA dataset demonstrate that the proposed method exceeds the performance of baseline models. Analysis of answers and rationales confirms the effectiveness of our approach, and the module's design facilitates the integration of different types of extracted knowledge.

Artificial Intelligence systems are increasingly deployed across various sectors, processing sensitive personal information. While these systems offer efficiency and accuracy, they are vulnerable to privacy attacks that can infer private data from their outputs. Although numerous privacy preservation techniques exist, most are designed for specific data processing models like data mining or machine learning, leaving a gap in strategies for general AI frameworks. This paper presents a coarse-to-grained privacy preservation approach based on knowledge graphs that leverages embedded world knowledge to restrict information release. We evaluate this strategy using the Social Question Answering (SQuAD) dataset. However, modeling their formation requires accurate reaction networks that remain constrained by limited, often conflicting, experimental data. This work examines experimental findings and theoretical calculations related to ion-molecule and neutral-molecule reactions involving three key species: OH+, H3O+, and CO+. In the Federated Linear Regression (FLR) context, existing methods often yield suboptimal sample complexities, a outcome we also demonstrate is asymptotically optimal. However, for general data distributions, current approaches are not. We propose \textit{FedLin}, a straightforward algorithm that achieves an even more optimal sample complexity. Beyond linear models, we investigate the generalization capabilities of fedted learning algorithms for non-linear models applied to data drawn from distributions belonging to the k-central Euclidean Clustering (k-EC) class. Although prior studies have established bounds for individual samples, they failed to determine a lower bound on the generalization error incurred by federated algorithms relative to a central learner. We define this metric as the Generalization Gap (GG), calculated as the difference between the excess risk of the federated model and that of the optimal model. We formulate and solve the problem of finding the minimax GG over the k-EC class, deriving matching upper and lower bounds. Our results indicate that the sample complexity required to close the GG for non-linear models on k-EC data is $\mathcal{O} \left( n \frac{n}{n+k} + \frac{n}{k} \log \frac{n}{k} \right)$. Notably, this complexity is intrinsic to the data distribution and does not depend on the specific complexity of the model class. We further obtain analogous results for the GG between a partial gradient descent model and the Bayes optimal model on Gaussian data. Our findings reveal that the sample complexities necessary to minimize the GG across various model complexities for data from the k-EC class are intrinsic. To support these conclusions, we present multiple numerical experiments. Drawing on North Carolina court data from 1994 to 2009, this study assesses whether mandating mental health treatment as a condition of probation reduces the probability of future re-offending. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis compares probationers ordered to undergo treatment against those who were not. The findings indicate that requiring treatment lowers the three-year recidivism rate by 5.6 percentage points, representing a 17 percent reduction. The impact is strongest in preventing future violent and property crimes, with effects intensifying over time following conviction. Furthermore, a cost-benefit analysis demonstrates that the reduction in crime generated by the treatment exceeds the expenses associated with providing it. Finally, the evidence suggests that mandating treatment is particularly effective for individuals with severe mental health issues who were previously avoiding medication or therapy. Policy implications are discussed regarding the use of randomized assignment mechanisms to strengthen evidence for mental health treatment mandates and the recommendation to require such treatment as a probation condition for suitable candidates.

This method employs a consistency regularization strategy that ensures the segmentation of interpolated pairs of unlabeled images aligns with the interpolation of their corresponding segmentation maps. As a form of data-adaptive regularization, it helps reduce overfitting to labeled data, particularly when confidence levels are high. Deep learning techniques have increasingly become a focal point for analyzing big health data. A primary application area is image analysis for medical diagnostics. However, the efficacy of these methods depends on the availability of hand-labeled training data, which is often limited. This paper introduces a new class of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) designed for multi-label classification of electron microscopy (EM) images from biological and medical samples. Our model integrates global context from color-histography-enhanced (CHH) feature maps and local patch-level features extracted from the middle layers of a ResNet-50 classifier-scaled aggregation module. The CHH maps are derived from extensive color-histography-engineered hand-labeled datasets. Furthermore, our GCN architecture incorporates a multi-scale patch aggregation module (MPAM) to handle varying patch sizes. This multi-scale capability allows the network to learn contextual relationships across different spatial resolutions, improving robustness and accuracy in classifying EM image patches for biologic/medical diagnostics. To evaluate the proposed model's ability to assess hierarchical multi-scale contexts in EM images, we developed a 10-class multi-label classification dataset using 1,500-pixel patches from EM electron nanoslicer images of myofibrils from healthy human cardiac tissue. Our GCN architecture was trained in a semi-supervised manner on this cardiology data. Benchmarking against state-of-the-art models shows that our approach significantly surpasses competitors in both accuracy and F1 scores across single-, multi-, and all-label classification tasks. how changes in local structural environments influence performance and longevity. In this work, we introduce a unified framework that extends beyond traditional average-based ensemble descriptors by utilizing joint probability distributions as general descriptors of both the electronic and nuclear ensembles. We implement this approach with post-processing resolution within time-discrete molecular dynamics (TDMD) simulations employing the joint distribution method (JDM). This technique enables the calculation of junction distribution changes (JDCs), which serve as representative measures of ensemble disruptions triggered by stressors like electric fields. These descriptors facilitate a direct mapping between dynamic, time-resolved, and local structural fluctuations and fluctuating electronic and optical properties, as property variations are governed by the underlying nuclear and electronic ensembles. This establishes a direct pathway to investigate the intricate dynamics of property degradation and aging. Furthermore, the proposed methodology offers a model-agnostic route to analyze the ensemble origins of property fluctuations and aging across various systems and theoretical frameworks, potentially offering insights unattainable through conventional analysis methods. To demonstrate the technique's capabilities, we examine the nonequilibrium dynamics and aging of amorphous aluminum under tension, comparing results against prior analyses based on structural clustering. The proposed method provides a transparent view of the complex relationship between ensemble disruptions and aging, relying on no model assumptions or pre-defined clustering choices. Consequently, this approach can be broadly applied to systems modeled by first-principles MD or coarse-grained models, including systems involving complex many-body effects described by advanced electronic structure theories. The technique delivers a clear and direct interpretation of the links between nuclear and electronic property fluctuations and aging and can be viewed as a sophisticated extension of differential scattering experiments. Ultimately, this offers a robust framework for analyzing the durability and aging mechanisms of atomic-scale systems in operational conditions using advanced simulation capabilities. The code is accessible at https://github.com/sohni-john/aging.

Like $\hat{H}_n^{new}$, our other estimator $\check{H}_n^{new}$ is also no less efficient than the jackknife estimator of Lo (2019). Both new estimators are at least as efficient as $\hat{H}_n$ of Lo (2017b). Specifically, $\check{H}_n^{new}$ surpasses $\hat{H}_n^{new}$ in terms of mean squared error for sample sizes $n \leq 150$. $P$ defined on any manifold $M$ possesses a closed range for its range operator ${\rm Re}_M P$ and a compact resolvent. Furthermore, if $M$ is compact, then ${\rm Re}_M P$ is a Fredholm operator. These findings generalize results by Atiyah and Singer, indicating that $P$ is Fredholm when $M$ is compact. The primary instrument in these proofs is a new proof of the Fredholm property, which depends on the ellipticity of $P$ at the boundary of $M$. Specifically, we utilize a characterization of the Fredholm property through the Fredholm alternative and the Gelfand–Shilov theorem on the solvability of adjoint operators. Notably, our demonstration of the closed range property for ${\rm Re}_M P$ bypasses the need for a Lopatinski\u0119 condition, a requirement typically necessary when $M$ has a boundary. Our manifold $M$ may be non-compact, possess boundaries, and may even be odd-dimensional. To achieve this, we employ a characterization of the Fredholm property based on the closed range of the real part and compactness of the resolvent. This characterization relies on characterizing the closed range via the Gelfand–Shilov theorem applied to the adjoint operator. Additionally, we provide an alternative approach using a different characterization of the closed range, which employs the Cramer rule for bounded operators on Banach spaces. SMT solver veriT was introduced a decade ago at the inaugural PxTP workshop. Since that time, the format has evolved significantly. veriT proofs are now employed in various applications, and other solvers also produce proofs using this standard. To inform future enhancements, we seek community feedback. In this process, we examine the format's history, outline our pragmatic development strategy, and address potential issues that may emerge when other solvers utilize the format. Ultimately, we invite comprehensive community review to guide further improvements. The full format specification is available on our website. We also provide a reference parser implemented in Rust, which can be accessed via Cargo. The parser is available as an independent tool for checking formatter output, or integrated as a component within veriT.

The \textit{FedBuff} algorithm (Nguyen et al., 2022) mitigates this issue by enabling asynchronous updates that tolerate staleness, thereby improving training scalability while maintaining privacy through secure aggregation. This paper revisits the \textit{FedBuff} algorithm for asynchronous federated learning, extending prior analysis by eliminating boundedness constraints on the gradient norm. It provides a theoretical examination of the algorithm's convergence rate under conditions of data heterogeneity, varying batch sizes, and communication delays. Furthermore, a laboratory-scale experiment on image classification with data heterogeneity validates the theoretical findings and illustrates the cost of any boundedness assumption regarding the gradient norm. Based on these outcomes, the research suggests potential directions for future work. Both the theoretical analysis and the empirical investigation are original and form the foundation of this research's contribution. Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Specifically, the final WER decreased from 9.4% to 8.4%, representing an 11% improvement, while training duration dropped by more than half, decreasing from 10 hours to under 5 hours.

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has seen substantial recent advancements through deep learning, particularly end-to-end neural models that map acoustic features directly to characters or subwords. These systems are increasingly popular for medium-sized tasks, such as those involving Catalan, which has a population of roughly 9 million. We present a robust end-to-end ASR architecture for Catalan that utilizes a sequence-to-sequence framework with convolutional encoder and decoder components. Our approach employs character-based representations to capture the morphological diversity of Catalan. Experiments conducted across three datasets yield a test WER of 6.1%. This result represents a significant leap forward, surpassing the prior best by 2 percentage points and demonstrating that our model trained exclusively on transcribed speech (without leveraging text data) now outperforms a system trained on combined speech and text datasets. Additionally, our findings indicate that character-based models are well-suited for medium-sized tasks. The code and models are publicly available.

Neural machine translation systems trained on large parallel corpora have recently advanced significantly. We investigate whether these models can learn morphology from monolingual target-language data, a scenario where vast parallel resources are unattainable. To address this, we formulate a transfer learning task: adapting a English-German translator to Czech, a country with a population of approximately 10.5 million. Our experiments yield two key insights. First, a model trained end-to-end on Czech achieves a test set WER of 8.4%. approach designed to tackle key challenges in robot navigation within marine environments. To enhance data efficiency, the method integrates TD updates with Gaussian Process regression. To facilitate online predictions, we propose a sparse approximation that offers superior quality compared to existing rejection-based techniques. By deriving the predictive value function posterior and utilizing its moments, we develop SPGP-SARSA, a novel algorithm for model-free policy evaluation. We further demonstrate that SPGP-SARSA can be easily adapted into its model-based equivalent, SPGP-TD. Through extensive simulations and physical trials with an underwater robot, our results indicate that SPGP-SARSA surpasses current state-of-the-art sparse methods, matches the prediction accuracy of its exact counterpart, and effectively solves underwater navigation tasks. Additionally, the algorithm successfully operates in scenarios involving dynamic obstacles. SPGP-SARSA is readily available at https://github.com/andrewjromero/romero-rsn.

ariant semi-tetrad method to model a general, static, and spherically symmetric relativistic star composed of two fluids exhibiting anisotropic pressure. This approach yields the corresponding covariant Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations for anisotropic conditions. These equations are subsequently employed to derive new exact solutions through direct resolution and reconstruction methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that three generating theorems established for single-fluid systems can also be applied to generate two-fluid solutions from single-fluid counterparts. Additionally, we examine specific features of co-evolving two-fluid systems and assess their feasibility based on energy conditions. The analysis and restrictions imposed by the first and second laws of thermodynamics on these systems are further explored. Finally, we investigate the stability of the obtained two-fluid solutions using the generalized causal Jordan-Gross-Pitaevsky criterion. All analytical findings are supported by graphical representations. Notably, the two fluids are not restricted to thermal equilibrium; one can drive the other away from its equilibrium state. Concretely, we demonstrate that a charged perfect fluid can be in thermal equilibrium with a heating anisotropic fluid, or two charging anisotropic fluids can maintain equilibrium with each other. In the latter scenario, the presence of mutual heating and cooling effects violates the zeroth law of thermodynamics. These results contrast with previous studies on two-fluid systems by highlighting the rich physical behaviors and complex constraints inherent in such configurations. Our graphical analyses complement existing literature and confirm the viability of the solutions. Overall, this research underscores the value of the covariant semi-tetrad method in deriving exact two-fluid solutions and demonstrates that key theorems from single-fluid systems remain effective for generating solutions in more complex environments.

This paper reframes distinct GEC domains as separate tasks and introduces a meta-learning framework for few-shot domain adaptation that requires no pseudo data. By leveraging data-rich source domains, we learn model parameter initializations that enable rapid adaptation to new, resource-constrained target domains. Specifically, we adapt the GEC model to the first language (L1) of second-language learners. Our evaluation utilizes nine source and three target domains, including the most widely used L1 learner data (FLORES-101). Experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot domain adaptation techniques across various settings. Furthermore, our approach surpasses data-overfitting baselines utilizing pseudo data and achieves superior results compared to traditional zero-shot domain adaptation methods in several scenarios. The core contribution of this work lies in demonstrating that meta-learning serves as an effective solution for few-shot domain adaptation in the L1 learner context. Source code is available at: https://github.com/ElhamShenashaneh/L1-MetaLearning.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently achieved major breakthroughs by integrating textual and visual information. Building on this success, this study develops a novel MLLM capable of answering medical questions through a medical dialogue interface, leveraging domain-specific few-shot data. Our evaluations indicate that the proposed model performs competitively against state-of-the-art approaches. However, training this model is computationally demanding due to its reliance on extensive pretraining and fine-tuning processes using large-scale, multimodal datasets. To address this challenge, we introduce an efficient framework designed to accelerate the training of MLLMs for medical dialogue systems. Despite using approximately 20 times less data and reducing training time by over 60 percent, our method yields superior results compared to traditional strategies. Specifically, when evaluated on a five-question medical dialogue dataset, our approach outperforms the Medialgo model by a margin of 7.11%, surpasses the Llama-2-chat baseline by 6.44%, and exceeds the Qwen-chat model by 5.19%. Source code is available at: https://github.com/ElhamShenashaneh/MedialDial. While this study focuses on the first language (L1) of second-language learners, the method is equally applicable to other medical domains

Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), ultimately providing an affirmative answer. We analyze two algorithms recognized for generating such allocations in non-strategic environments: Round-Robin, which yields EF1 allocations for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method by Plaut and Roughgarden [SIAM J. Discrete Math. 31(4):1952--1978, 2017] that produces EFX allocations for two agents. We demonstrate that all pure Nash equilibria of Round-Robin result in allocations that are EF1 relative to the agents' true values. Furthermore, we introduce and examine a generalized Round-Robin algorithm that also yields EF1 allocations strategically. Additionally, we prove that the "give-tops" algorithm by Su [Math. Oper. Res. 48(2):708--733, 2023] generates EFX allocations in a strategic setting. However, no mechanism can simultaneously satisfy two conditions: (i) being strategyproof for all valuations and (ii) always yielding pure Nash equilibria. Similarly, it is impossible for a mechanism to be both strategyproof and produce EF1 allocations for two agents with cardinal utilities. Regarding the feasibility of pure Nash equilibria for EF1 allocations across three or more agents with quasi-linear utilities, we show that such a scenario is unattainable if the number of indivisible items is not divisible by the number of agents. For the "give-tops" algorithm, this implies that any deviation by an agent can cause the total utility of all other agents to decrease without bound. Conversely, both the Round-Robin and algorithms by Plaut and Roughgarden fail to produce EF1 allocations for three or more agents with quadratic utilities when the number of items is not divisible by the number of agents. By comparing UGC 8839 with three similar spiral galaxies—UGC 8835, UGC 8837, and UGC 8843—we find that all five share nearly identical global properties when analyzed through their outer disks. This study examines how our results vary with quark mass and evaluates the significance of correlations between the quark and antiquark inside the pion. The method presented in this paper is directly applicable to examining other quark correlations, such as those between quarks and heavy antiquarks (e.g., charm or bottom) in mesons and baryons. Our lattice data for quark-quark correlations in pions align well with chiral perturbation theory predictions. We also present quark mass dependencies for proton quark correlations, which can be validated against future lattice QCD results. Lattice QCD offers distinct advantages over quark models for studying these correlations. Regarding previous lattice studies on protons, our work differs by providing a comprehensive analysis of quark mass dependencies, employing a larger number of ensembles, and achieving a more precise signal quality for the $ud$ correlation in protons. Lattice QCD results for quark quanta in protons contradict recent quark model studies, while lattice results for quark quanta in pions agree with quark model findings. Lattice QCD results for quark quanta in protons also disagree with recent analyses of quark momentum distributions in protons based on global properties of proton charge radii. Lattice QCD results for quark quanta in protons further contrast with recent quark model analyses of quark momentum distributions in protons. analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly considered. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha across multiple observations. These variations can influence interpretations of data from surveys like TW Hese. Furthermore, significant fluctuations in XX Cha's accretion will impact models of star and disk evolution, as well as the inferred properties of its population. We observed XX Cha on three occasions over approximately 1.5 years, measuring time-resolved variable accretion rates of $\sim$ few $\times$ $10^{-8}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr, $\sim$ $10^{-7}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr, and $\sim$ $3\times$ $10^{-7}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr. The variations between the first two observations account for more than 99 percent of the total dispersion in inferred ages for XX Cha. Transient accretion events, lasting at least one day, were detected in the H$\alpha$ line profile of XX Cha. These events involved increases in accretion power ranging from 10 to 30 percent, with no obvious correlation to the line profile morphology or specific event durations. Based on the target's activity and the length of our monitoring period, the time-averaged mass accretion rate is $\sim$ $(1.0\pm0.1)\times$ $10^{-7}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr, corresponding to an age of $\sim$ 12 Myr using the viscosity-driven model of disk evolution from \citet{flock16}. This age represents a factor of two reduction compared to estimates derived from assuming constant accretion. The events in XX Cha do not follow the positive or negative feedback mechanisms described by the TW Herbig Ae/Be feedback model (Flock2016, 2019); they are stochastic, and the resulting disk evolution timescales vary by orders of magnitude depending on the specific event properties. Consequently, these transient events can significantly alter the inferred ages of disks. Ultimately, accurate assessment of protoplanetary disk evolution requires time-variable mass accretion rates, as ignoring them can lead to substantial discrepancies in derived physical parameters

However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared-Reward Multi-policy Learning (SRML). SRML aims to discover a common suboptimal behavior across all agents by leveraging their respective offline data, thereby enhancing the performance of the entire system. Specifically, SRML operates under the assumption that each agent's offline data was collected using a distinct behavior policy. By integrating potential reward maximization techniques with a cross-entropy method, we design algorithms that explore the potential superior behavior of agents by analyzing their individual offline datasets. These behaviors are then optimized through the maximization of a global reward. Evaluations across diverse partial and full-observation multi-agent particle environments demonstrate that SRML significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, a ablation study provides insights into the design of each component within the SRML framework. SRML represents an open endeavor, and its codebase will be made publicly available. conference, Einstein advocated for an absolute time framework, arguing that conventional physics could only proceed by disregarding its relativistic implications. Twelve years later, he demonstrated that his earlier arguments could be applied to thermodynamics, concluding that statistical mechanics relies on absolute time and that the second law of thermodynamics is fundamentally false. This paper revisits the 1939 Solvay meeting to examine the evolution of Einstein's thoughts on the first and second laws of thermodynamics and their respective implications for the nature of time. The analysis also considers how these perspectives challenge the standard interpretation of the first law regarding energy conservation. Furthermore, we present support for the claim that a time-independent formulation of the first law is possible when rooted in Newtonian rather than relativistic physics, and that the second law represents the most robust indication that time is not absolute. The study concludes by addressing common misconceptions surrounding the first law and proposing that these concepts be re-introduced into physics education. Since the first and second laws of thermodynamics reflect the most basic properties of time, understanding them offers significant value for interpreting both standard and emerging phenomena in various fields, including physics, chemistry, biology, and social sciences.

During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile station (MS) without transferring the codebook; the MS then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MS, as it relies on the UL data to determine the selected entry. The number of codebook entries is defined by the count of GMM components, which can be adjusted based on the size of the UL training dataset to optimize feedback rate and complexity. Crucially, this approach requires no cooperation between the BS and MS for training data collection, as the GMM is trained solely on UL measurements. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms conventional codebook generation and clustering techniques, particularly in high-mobility scenarios and when utilizing large training datasets. Overall, the system design is highly efficient, and the feedback encoding process is both simple and low-complexity. The system's high effectiveness stems from its ability to accurately estimate the distribution of UL training data through GMMs and its adoption of a clustering strategy that distributes codebook entries uniformly across this distribution. We present a framework to establish the permanence of 2D robust Prandtl boundary layers, yielding the first example of a permanent robust crosscurrent in the forced Navier-Stokes equations. Our method involves generating a system of permanence equations via an asymptotic expansion, followed by the permanence analysis of a specific system of partial differential inequalities featuring a quasilinear questionably homogeneous structure. This result implies the emergence of (quasi-)Lie symmetry for the permanence system, which facilitates the explicit calculation of all (first lying) integrating factors and (quasi-)Lie symmetries for the entire system. These computations allow for the direct application of Dafermos' method to derive the permanence of the solution. To ensure the solution remains well-defined, we impose conditions on the initial data that are both necessary and sufficient. Furthermore, this permanence guarantees the asymptotic behavior of the solution at infinity, a requirement essential for the solution to represent a turbulent eddy. This paper thus establishes the foundational model of a 2D robust Prandtl boundary layer and provides a pathway to model 2D turbulent eddies. Key components of this work may find applications in other fields where asymptotic expansions are utilized. Specifically, this is achieved by permanence analyzing PDEs with a quasilinear questionably homogeneous structure in system form—a finding that is of independent significance. This is accomplished by extending the classical theory of questionably homogeneous functions to system form and developing new techniques to determine (quasi-)Lie symmetry for system differential equations, thereby ensuring the permanence of the solution. Consequently, this represents a significant advancement over previous studies, which had only achieved such permanence for system differential inequalities. Long and short-term memory (LSTM) networks have recently achieved significant success in natural language processing. However, their complex architecture leads to high computational costs, making real-time inference challenging on mobile and embedded systems. This paper introduces LSTM-Squeeze (LMS), a highly efficient LSTM model achieved via intelligent parameter pruning. The core idea of LMS is to reduce both the memory footprint and computation count of standard LSTM networks by eliminating redundant parameters. Experimental results on the WikiNews, WikiQA, TED, and IWSLT translation tasks show that LMS uses approximately one-third of the memory of a full-sized LSTM on a mobile CPU while maintaining similar accuracy and requiring less time for inference. Additionally, LMS exceeds the one-second inference threshold on a mobile CPU for the WikiNews task. Because LMS preserves the memory efficiency and training feasibility of LSTMs and excels at transfer learning, it is ideally suited for mobile and edge applications. Our LMS model can be easily deployed using existing lightweight models such as MobileNet and Transformer Encoder. Like the original LSTM, LMS is well-suited for acceleration on neural network-specific hardware like GPUs and TPUs. To facilitate the widespread adoption of LMS in real-world scenarios, we provide an official implementation and encourage researchers to develop further optimization strategies, such as knowledge distillation and quantization. Finally, we release the LMS network structure and a pre-trained WikiNews model for public use. The official code and models are accessible at https://lingdustt.github.io/LMS/.

This analysis examines the necessity of such conditions when gravitational self-force corrections are incorporated. Specifically, for $SU(N)$ fundamental electrons, self-force corrections are strictly positive, implying that the standard conjecture holds without modification. Conversely, anti-fundamental electrons exhibit positive self-force only at next-to-leading order; their leading-order effect is negative, suggesting these states should also be excluded to maintain consistency with the conjecture. Consequently, if the inclusion of anti-fundamental electrons is mandatory, the conjecture must be reformulated. This implies a lower bound on maximum charge-to-mass ratios, potentially indicating the existence of a minimum non-zero mass for irreducible representations of $SU(N)$. Within a potential string theory framework where global symmetries are approximated by local ones and $U(1)$ charges correspond to representation weights, the necessity of both minimal weights and non-BPS black hole states becomes apparent. Furthermore, the magnitude of self-force corrections implies that any such state must have a Compton wavelength at least as large as the Schwarzschild radius, or else it would undergo gravitational collapse into an extremal black hole. Finally, we contrast this with the CW conjecture regarding $SO(d)$, which, unlike the Weak Gravity Conjecture, does not require the exclusion of states with the largest charge-to-mass ratio; instead, it mandates the presence of two distinct branches of states, one increasing and the other decreasing with decreasing mass. We explore the implications of these findings for the landscape of string vacua. Additionally, we address the application of these concepts to global symmetries and discuss how the behavior of self-force corrections could influence ideas surrounding holographic fine-tuning. In the appendices, we detail our computational approach to calculating self-force corrections and examine the gravity-only limit of our equations.

Under these conditions, a unitary operator exists that commutes with the Hamiltonian, allowing for the construction of a complex-valued Lorentzian metric which renders the system Hamiltonian outside the obstacle region. Consequently, a real Hamiltonian can be defined that is unitarily equivalent to the original Hamiltonian for any value of $\lambda$. Additionally, a relationship is established showing how the value of $\lambda$ corresponds to a unitary transformation between the two equivalent Hamiltonians. Numerical investigations for various complex values of $\lambda$ reveal an abundance of exceptional points and exceptional curves. Ultimately, the findings for $\lambda \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0,1\}$ provide support for the existence of a family of Lorentzian metrics that are Hamiltonian with respect to the Schrödinger equation for any complex $\lambda$, despite the presence of a mass-supersingular connection. These results offer insights into the complexity arising from mass-supersingular transformations within the context of the Schrödinger equation and support the feasibility of bypassing such singularities via complex-valued mass-supersingular metrics. The significance of these discoveries is highlighted against the backdrop of recent advancements in black hole physics.

Such results are essential for transferring theorems from commutative algebra between characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic contexts. The author further establishes a comparable theorem based on a more intricate class of reductions, which yields comparable theorems for significant structural results in commutative algebra, including Hilbertianity, Hilbert's Irreducibility Theorem, and Kronecker's Theorem. These findings generalize previous work by the author and B. Poonen. The proposed complexity class offers a permissive framework that retains sufficient structure to enable trans-characteristic theorems while avoiding the exclusivity of prior approaches; this is achieved by allowing finite sets of obstructions at specific prime ideals of the ambient ring over which irreducibility is assessed. Key applications include a novel, concise proof of the trans-characteristic version of Hilbertianity and Hilbert's Irreducibility Theorem as presented by B. Reznick, improving upon previous proofs by the author, offering a shorter demonstration of the trans-characteristic Hilbertianity of regular rings due to D. Harbater and the author, and providing a new, brief proof of the trans-characteristic Hilbertianity of multivariate power series rings, as established by the author and R. Frixione. A primary objective of this line of research is to identify the minimal necessary complexity of reductions over finite fields to facilitate theorem transfer, and this paper explores several directions for future investigation. The results presented were previously featured in the dissertation of the author from Tel Aviv University. The core findings of this study were also the subject of the thesis by B. Reznick at Tel Aviv University. Trans-characteristic Hilbertianity and its applications can be found in the thesis of R. Frixione at Ben-Gurion University. A concise overview of the research presented here was delivered as a talk at the "Arithmetic, Geometry, and Cryptography" conference in Tel Aviv on June 19, 2023. We provide a complete characterization of this functor's image, demonstrating that it yields a subcategory of $k$-fold vector bundles comprising symmetric structures equipped with a family of morphisms indexed by the symmetric group ${\mathbb S}_k$. Notably, in the degree 2 case, this added structure defines a symplectical double vector bundle, representing the skew-symmetric counterpart to a metric double vector bundle. Furthermore, we examine the related scenario of fully linearising $N$-manifolds and illustrate how the full linearisation functor enables the "superisation" of a graded bundle. These findings have significant applications within the framework of relative (super)geometry. Additionally, we introduce and fully describe the notion of a connection on a graded bundle, offering a detailed analysis of the corresponding connection operators. Notably, this type of connection enables the construction of the graded (super) Tangent bundle from its classical counterpart. Finally, we briefly explore morphisms between graded bundles and their linearisations, as well as vertical and invective maps. All concepts and results presented are accompanied by examples. This work serves as an introduction to the field of graded bundles and is intended to function as a reference for the underlying terminology. Keywords: graded bundle, linealisation, vector bundle, double vector bundle, symplectical double vector bundle, Bernoulli connection, tangent bundle, supermanifold. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 53B50, 58E05, 58D10.

While confocal microscopy offers high spatial resolution, it is constrained by the diffraction limit, which affects both focus and collection. Collection is particularly limiting, often necessitating near-field approaches to achieve nanometric volumes. This study introduces a technique that achieves nanometric spatial resolution using collection-unconstrained bulk samples through the analysis of polarization modifications induced by a nanometric volume on bulk polarization. The method's feasibility was validated using a 3D object, and nanometric volume selection was confirmed via collection-unconstrained nonlinear microscopy. Although this approach does not reduce the diffraction limit, it achieves a nanometric volume for interaction, making it especially valuable when sample damage or photobleaching are concerns. Furthermore, the volume selection is collection-unconstrained, allowing for deep focusing, and can be easily adapted to achieve 2D nanometric spot selection. This collection-unconstrained bulk volume selection is particularly beneficial in deep ultraviolet (DUV) confocal microscopy, where spatial resolution is currently compromised by both interaction and collection. By leveraging existing DUV collection optics without sacrificing volume selection, this approach reduces the interaction volume to approximately 10 µm³, which is roughly 1000 times smaller than in current DUV confocal microscopy. Consequently, this enables a significant decrease in the signal from the out-of-focus volume in 3D structures, enhancing DUV confocal spatial resolution by a factor of 10 in both x and y dimensions. Although the proposed technique is application-specific, its core principle of collection-unconstrained bulk volume selection is broadly applicable to other domains, potentially achieving even smaller interaction volumes. Ultimately, this method improves confocal spatial resolution in the x, y, and z directions by a factor of 1000 within the 280–330 nm wavelength range, which is critical for lithography, nano-imprinting, and forensics. Unlike other collection-unconstrained bulk volume selection techniques, this is the first to include 3D volume selection and, unlike collection-unconstrained focus deformation methods, it does not compromise spatial resolution in the x and y directions. Unlike other DUV confocal microscopy collection-unconstrained focus deformation methods, the proposed technique reduces the interaction volume from milliliters to ~10 µm³. Although not every component is novel, the application is original, and the principle is both innovative and simple. Ultimately, this is the first method to reduce both the interaction and total DUV

applied to the incompressible Darcy-Forchheimer system, which models low Reynolds number flows featuring significant non-linear effects. The proposed approach decouples velocity and pressure: pressure is approximated by a lowest-order convex element, while pressure-gradient velocity is assigned an independent higher-order space than the pressure. The analysis demonstrates that multiple weak solutions exist when the pressure is within the closure of the cone of non-negative pressures under the $L^2$ norm. Furthermore, the study establishes the uniqueness of the weak solution (specifically, the pressure) within the closure of the pressure class defined by the corresponding norm. These findings mirror those of low-dimensional stationary incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Additionally, a novel regularity result for pressure is derived, stating that if the pressure belongs to $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ for some $1\leq p<2$, it is superharmonic and thus belongs to $W^{1,q}(\Omega)$ for all $q\in [1, \infty)$. The convergence of the proposed hybrid-mixed method is examined, with rates established for pressure, velocity gradient, and velocity (the latter depending on the Sobolev regularity of the pressure). These convergence rates were previously unproven. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and illustrate the observed convergence rates. The results regarding pressure regularity and method convergence are examined in the context of surface reconstruction for velocity, particularly in relation to the no-slip condition. The analysis also considers the transition from Darcy flow to Navier-Stokes flow as the viscosity parameter $\varepsilon$ approaches zero, with similar behaviors noted near the obstacle. However, the transition to Darcy flow is analyzed in detail, revealing that the solution converges to the unique non-trivial, positive, odd, $C^{1}(\mathbb{R}\setminus \{0\})$ solution of the Hiemenz flow as it approaches a boundary layer. This was achieved by formulating the problem near the obstacle to resemble the Hiemenz problem and utilizing previous analysis results. Finally, the connection between the Darcy-Forchheimer flow past an obstacle and the Hiemenz flow is explored through the existence of a pressure gradient along the symmetry axis of the obstacle.

science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data. Although Bayes factors provide a direct measure for comparing hypotheses, they lack a standard scale for classification; typically, approximate mappings to p-values are used, a process that remains controversial. In this paper, we evaluate several proposed scale mappings and introduce a novel scale grounded in decision theory. However, these scales remain suitable only for specific, simple pairs of hypothesis values. For complex values, we demonstrate that a simple rule relying on the continuity correction of the positive part of the log-Bayes factor is optimal. This rule categorizes evidence as strong, moderate, weak, or none, yet it remains inconclusive regarding the direction of the effect. We provide R packages implementing all described methods, which are also accessible via CRAN. The source code for the optimal rule is available on GitHub. Our findings indicate that rejecting the null hypothesis corresponds to strong or moderate evidence of an effect, rejecting alternative hypotheses aligns with strong or clear evidence against an effect, and a Bayes factor greater than one signifies at least weak evidence. Evidence is deemed strong when the probability of data favoring the opposite conclusion is below 5%. Ultimately, we aim to minimize errors in both concluding an effect exists when it does not, and failing to recognize an effect that does exist. (R packages `hypothes testing` and `hypothes testing decision` are required for Reproducility Supplement 1 and 2.) (Code for the optimal rule is accessible at: https://github.com/hv001/EvidenceCategories). (Reproducility Supplement 1 and 2 are available at: https://osf.io/y354a). Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize the capacity to predict discourse markers before sentence classification to derive improved models for sentiment analysis and parodic character classification. Specifically, we formulate classification-relevant tasks using character-defining discourse markers extracted from genre- and character-appropriate corpora. Our experimental results on parodic character classification in comments (Twitter and YouTube) and movie reviews demonstrate significant accuracy improvements across sentiment analysis for annotated parodic characters and parodic character classification itself. Furthermore, we provide evidence that our approach yields accurate parodic character classifiers even when the assigned characters are inferred from the model's sentiment predictions rather than being explicitly defined during training. Finally, we release our dataset of discourse markers associated with parodic characters, which can facilitate future research in this field. Our findings suggest that hand-cored character definitions are not strictly necessary for achieving high accuracy in parodic character classification and that such characters are inherently identifiable through models trained only on sentiment. Our experiments indicate that strategically chosen discourse markers contain rich information about both the sentiment and the parodic characters within a dataset. Consequently, incorporating these markers as additional inputs before the final classification layer can lead to significant accuracy gains, even when the model lacks explicit training on parodic character assignment. We advocate for the generalizability of our approach across a broad spectrum of parodic character classification scenarios and in contexts involving a lexicon of character-defining words. Experimental results on a sentiment analysis task involving named entities yield similar outcomes to those observed with discourse markers. However, we note the existence of specific "cheating" strategies for named entity classification that can also account for the accuracy improvements seen in our parodic character classification task. We hope our work offers a pragmatic and broadly applicable framework for applying discourse markers beyond the domain of parodic character classification. Our methodology can serve as a straightforward and effective procedure for any sentence classification task where a relevant discourse marker lexicon is available. We believe this is particularly common in tasks where entities representing categories are inserted into text, such as named entity classification, product attribute classification, or coreference resolution.

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (RSC), where local linear algorithms converge linearly; (RSC'), exhibiting similar convergence properties to (RSC); and (not-RSC'), characterized by a large radius of convergence. These findings rely on a key insight: the standard RSC condition remains preserved under the factorized objective despite the objective not being strictly convex. Furthermore, we establish that the radius of convergence for standard RSC is at least $1/\sqrt{\kappa}$, where $\kappa$ denotes the condition number of the objective. Finally, our results indicate that the global landscape of the factorized objective is relatively simple, suggesting that local algorithms are likely to find a global minimizer. These conclusions are supported by numerical experiments. Our work contributes to the growing field of landscape analysis for the Burer-Monteiro factorization, particularly regarding global landscape assessments. This research extends our earlier research report [20]. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/hiyoshi1228/psd-rsc-bm.

Our introduced "social-learning" variants successfully establish this equilibrium, whereas "individual learning" versions fail to converge strategies to the Nash outcome. When players utilize "canonical co-evolutionary genetic algorithms," the game dynamics form an ergodic Markov Chain; consequently, we analyze simulation results using transition matrices, stationary distributions, and their corresponding Nash Equilibria. Furthermore, an LaTeX source code file details a statistical hypothesis test designed to compare the states of the Markov Chains generated by these algorithms. This test utilizes Lyapunov exponents to determine whether competing strategies evolve identically or diverge based on their posterior probabilities. The hypothesis test validates that simulations indicate "social learning" produces Nash Equilibrium strategies, while "individual learning" does not. Additionally, Kaplan-Meier estimates of survival functions for strategy states reveal that "social learning" outcomes are significantly more likely to reach the Nash Equilibrium than "individual learning" outcomes. We also examine the entropy of these survival functions to quantify the uncertainty and complexity of the simulations. Finally, the study examines the application of "memetic algorithms" to accelerate player learning within the Cournot game framework. Keywords: Co-evolutionary genetic algorithms, Cournot game, Entropy, Hypothesis test, Kaplan-Meier estimate, Markov Chains, Nash Equilibrium, Simulation, Statistical analysis, "Social learning". 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 91A43, 68T50, 62P20.

This paper establishes that for a specific class of weighted oriented trees, the ordinary and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ are identical. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which the ordinary and symbolic powers coincide for naturally oriented lines. Symbolic powers were initially introduced by Brodmann in 1979 to investigate the stability of associated primes and local cohomology modules of local rings. Since then, this topic has attracted significant attention from various perspectives (see, for example, and the references within). However, most existing studies focus on polynomial rings and commutative monomial ideals. In contrast, research on graph-related ideals, particularly those involving oriented graphs, remains limited. Notably, there are no existing studies examining the ordinary and symbolic powers of generalized edge ideals for such ideals.

now integral to many safety-critical computer vision tasks, such as automated driving and human-robot interaction. To ensure safety, these systems must adhere to specific constraints, typically enforced by verifying that input perturbations within a defined norm do not cause violations of safety properties. Recent safety assurance techniques involve searching for the maximal norm ball centered at any location on the $N$-dimensional signal space that results in a classification change or violates a safety property (a counterexample). These methods are particularly valuable for deviating adversarially from real-world traffic signals and signs. This paper evaluates current assurance strategies across various noise models relevant to weather conditions, camera obstructions, and lens reflections. We demonstrate that existing techniques often fail to align with these practical noise models, as they can exploit localized errors rather than distributed ones. To address this, we propose a framework of meta-optimization techniques designed to prioritize solutions under specified input noise models, thereby creating more realistic attack scenarios. Evaluations with multiple weather and reflection models show significant improvements, indicating that state-of-the-art safety assurance for CNNs can be strengthened against these realistic disturbances. The proposed framework is open-source, flexible, and readily adaptable to other practical deployment conditions. The code is available at: https://github.com/ItayGashavi/reflect.

Integrating deep reinforcement learning (DRL) into control systems for safety-critical processes is increasingly common, yet their safety remains difficult to guarantee. Formally, the goal is to ensure system trajectories satisfy temporal logic specifications despite uncertainties in initial states, plant dynamics, and the learning algorithm itself. We introduce a novel approach to assess the safety of model-free DRL systems by analyzing the largest uncertainty ball around the initial state (the verifiable safe set) where the system is assured to remain until a target set is reached without violating a given safety specification. This set is determined by solving a constrained Markov decision process (MDP) optimization where the objective is minimized safety value (rather than maximized reward) subject to safety constraints. Unlike current methods based on the robust value function, our uncertainty quantification is based on the belief state, offering two advantages: it avoids double sampling uncertainty and provides an exact characterization of state-wise initial condition uncertainty, unlike the time-dependent robust value function which characterizes distribution uncertainty. Extending beyond simple word alignment, we implement multiple cluster-level alignments, ensuring that word clusters maintain consistent distributions across different languages. Our clustering strategy leverages three distinct signals: (1) neighboring words within monolingual embedding spaces, (2) character-level data, and (3) linguistic properties such as part-of-speech tags and morphological features. We evaluate the quality of our cluster-aligned spaces using multiple quality indicators and compare results against single-alignment baseline models. Furthermore, we assess the generalization capability of our cluster-aligned cross-lingual spaces by applying them to downstream tasks, including loan translation, parallel sentence creation, and multilingual classification. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields significant gains in these applications compared to monolingual or baseline cross-lingual embedding spaces. The resulting cluster-aligned multilingual embedding spaces offer researchers and NLP practitioners a valuable new resource for enhancing low-resource languages. Additionally, our method is easily adaptable to cross-lingual task-specific modeling. The implementation is available at https://github.com/hamshad10/CL-MultiClusterSE. on, (anti-)proton, and $\phi$ meson production at midrapidity in Xe-Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV. Transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) spectra and integrated yields are derived across various centrality bins, ranging from pp to Pb-Pb collisions, organized by XeXecutor executor configurations. When benchmarked against similar experiments at comparable collision energies, pion and kaon spectra from XeXecutor collisions exhibit characteristics of both peripheral AA encounters and medium-free nuclear interactions, specifically showing enhanced radial flow and modified spectral shapes. Anti-protons display significantly greater suppression than protons across all $p_{\rm T}$ ranges, a phenomenon attributed to interaction within the quark-gluon plasma. The suppression of the $\phi$ meson at higher $p_{\rm T}$ is linked to its interaction with the quark-gluon plasma. The findings from ee collisions suggest that anti-proton production is suppressed relative to expectations based on hadron-hadron interactions, likely due to interactions with the quark-gluon plasma. Notably, in central XeXecutor collisions, the ratio of anti-protons to protons is lower than in peripheral encounters, indicating that anti-baryon production becomes increasingly suppressed as density rises. Additionally, the suppression of $\phi$ mesons is more pronounced in central collisions compared to central ee collisions. The data further reveal that as executor centralities increase, both the transverse flow and hadonization temperature of the quark-gluon plasma decline. Ultimately, this analysis offers insights into transverse flow and hadronization mechanisms within the quark-gluon plasma at intermediate energies. The reported results provide essential references for transporting hadrons and mesons in the quark-gluon plasma and for understanding hadronization and freeze-out at moderate energies.

9, Chile, particularly its capital Santiago, experienced extensive violence that resulted in the destruction of both public and private infrastructure. This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. These findings underscore the necessity of integrating key elements driving the spatial evolution of riots, such as population movement and infrastructure damage, to create effective models capable of replicating the true spatial distributions of disorder. Ultimately, this research offers a novel framework for analyzing future episodes of civil unrest.

Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. . Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant attention due to their strong performance. These methods train a neural network to process data from conventional filter-based VIO systems, utilizing output states and measurements as inputs to estimate camera poses via end-to-end learning. This paper investigates deep learning VIO to determine the appropriate complexity level for different scenarios. Since high network complexity risks overfitting in data-sparse situations and excessive parameters increase computational costs, we first compare the learning capabilities of various network sizes across multiple Scenarios (A through F), each containing a distinct number of data frames. This comparison identifies the maximum recommended network complexity for each scenario, ensuring optimal performance without overfitting. Building on these findings, we then evaluate different data enhancement techniques, including re-sampling, repetition, and interpolation, to maximize the usable dataset size and expand Scenario G. Finally, we assess learning performance using representative network sizes, applying relevant interpolation methods while maintaining low complexity to minimize computational overhead. Our experimental results indicate that deep learning VIO performance surpasses that of traditional filters, particularly in scenarios with large baseline distances where perspective distortion is more pronounced. Additionally, the use of enhancement techniques significantly improves learning outcomes, allowing accurate estimation even with extended data ranges. Overall, accurate and cost-effective VIO can be achieved by selecting network complexity suited to the available data. To support this, we have released the datasets and evaluation code used in this study on GitHub.

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our findings reveal that SHOWS supports both "Fermi-arc" surface states and hinge states linking the projections of Weyl points. We successfully constructed this exotic SHOWS state theoretically and observed it experimentally in three-dimensional (3D) stacked electric circuits featuring honeycomb-kagome hybridizations and double-helix interlayer couplings. These results pave the way for achieving square-root topology within 3D solid-state systems. The concept of square-root topology is not limited to SHOWS; it can potentially be extended to other square-root photonic and phononic systems, such as square-root Dirac and Weyl semimetals, as well as photo-elastic media exhibiting square-root Metamaterial transformations. Furthermore, we anticipate finding analogous phenomena in photo-elastic media, which are currently under investigation. Any theoretical breakthroughs in this field can be directly validated through experimental methods, as demonstrated here. Our theoretical framework is general and can be applied to identify and design exotic square-root photonic and phononic states of matter.

The discovery of topological phases has been significantly advanced by the formulation of topological invariants, which remain pivotal in modern research. However, the search for exotic phases continues, including those defined by non-integer invariants known as fractional topological phases. These phases, often termed "square-root topological phases," manifest as half-quantized surface or hinge states in 3D square-root Hamiltonians, such as the square-root Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSHE) model. While these phases have been extensively studied in 1D and 2D platforms like photonic and phononic crystals, their exploration in 3D remains challenging due to complex structural requirements. Traditional approaches involving "Weyl-Higgs transitions," where Weyl points collapse into loops and then into lines of SHOWS states, are not the only mechanisms for generating square-root topology.

To overcome these challenges, we propose a general theoretical framework capable of identifying square-root topology in 3D systems without relying on specific formation mechanisms. We illustrate this by demonstrating the emergence of SHOWS in a specific 3D stacked circuit and in a 3D photonic crystal featuring a honeycomb-kagome honeycomb structure with distinct intra- and interlayer couplings. The proposed framework is broadly applicable to

The objective involves reconstructing missing information on the inaccessible portion of the boundary of a bounded domain using measurements obtained from the accessible part. The paper investigates the non-iterative quasi-reversibility method and introduces several mixed variational formulations. Proofs are provided for well-posedness, convergence, and regularity. FedSA), a novel knowledge-amalgamation problem aimed at training a student model using diverse, non-overlapping datasets distributed across participating parties without data sharing. Unlike traditional federated learning goals of training a shared student model that reaches the performance of the largest individual dataset, our objective is to create a student model that surpasses every other party's result, even when their datasets do not overlap. To ensure the student model exceeds each participant's output, we enforce lower bounds on a validation set for every party. We formulate this problem as an optimization task subject to adversarial robustness constraints, guaranteeing that the resulting student model outperforms any of the original datasets while adhering to performance floors across all validation sets. FedSA delivers a cutting-edge solution to this challenge through the NOVA algorithm, which ensures the student model matches the performance of each party's dataset (within a specified tolerance) without exceeding computational costs more than 3x that of training on a single dataset. To our knowledge, FedSA represents a new category of knowledge amalgamation; existing methods either fail to meet these rigorous criteria or incur excessive computational overheads. Empirical results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet confirm that NOVA successfully generates a student model that matches the performance of each party's dataset within a 1% tolerance. Additionally, we introduce a constrained variant of FedSA for scenarios where some performance tolerances are already defined, offering a linear speedup compared to conventional knowledge distillation on overlapping datasets. Finally, we outline potential applications of this work in real-world contexts. The source code is available at https://github.com/NoahZeydler/FedSA.

Federated learning enables collaborative model training across institutions that cannot share data. This paper proposes a framework for sharing pre-trained models where the goal is to create a combined model that surpasses any individual pre-trained model, even when no data overlap exists between parties. Utilizing a one-dimensional, time-dependent atmospheric model, we simulate a CO$_2$-dominated atmosphere with cloud formation and surface ocean interactions, followed by a separate model assessing radiative-equilibrium profiles across the full range of plausible atmospheric pressures. We determine that a pressure of approximately 30 bar yields the present-day radiative-equilibrium temperature profile, whereas lower pressures (1--10 bar) are unstable and prone to generating super-adiabatic gradients. Consequently, Venus would have required an atmospheric pressure between 1 and 30 bar to initiate the runaway greenhouse effect, a process estimated to take 700 to 1,100 years. Our simulations of this phenomenon, starting from conditions similar to modern Earth but lacking an ocean, indicate a timescale of roughly 3,000 years, which may be influenced by the absence of an initial ocean. Subsequent condensation into clouds and the formation of an surface ocean followed, potentially leaving Venus in the 30 bar radiative-equilibrium profile, which has likely persisted for billions of years. However, the photolytic escape of hydrogen from the upper atmosphere continues to warm the planet's interior, potentially driving resurfacing events every 300 to 700 million years. These findings were achieved without employing prespecified super-adiabatic processes, such as convection or turbulence. While this simplified model captures the onset and progression of runaway greenhouse timescales and the stable radiative-equilibrium characteristics, it may lack the complexity required to fully represent Venus's vigorous atmospheric circulation. Ultimately, the mass of Venus's current CO$_2$ atmosphere and its radiative-equilibrium temperature profile are consequences of planetary history, including the extent of water availability, the duration and intensity of runaway greenhouse episodes, escape mechanisms, and geochemical feedbacks. A more detailed model incorporating surface interactions and the geological history could offer greater precision in explaining the evolution of Venus's atmosphere. These results enhance our fundamental comprehension of planetary evolution and the physical processes shaping rocky worlds, while also refining estimates of habitable zone boundaries, which are now suggested to be closer to the Sun than previously thought, potentially excluding super-Earths and Earth-mass planets in this region from having surface liquid water.

Among these, Hawkes processes are particularly popular due to their capacity to represent both endogenous feedback and exogenous interactions within a compact framework. This study investigates the statistical learning of Hawkes processes from observed event data, specifically focusing on the impact of sampling frequency in discrete-time estimation methods. While sampling rates in real-world applications are often unknown, prior assumptions can constrain the performance of standard estimators. Multiple Hawkes processes offer a robust model for capturing a system of feedback and cross-excitations among distinct sources. This paper presents a new approach to fitting these processes to high-frequency event data. We introduce a working model based on observations at irregular intervals that accounts for unobserved initial states and measurement errors in the high-frequency data. The model parameters are estimated via an EM algorithm using exact likelihoods derived from the underlying high-frequency process. Applications were tested on synthetic data and datasets of goal events from three football matches and seismic data from the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake aftershocks. In both cases, the results indicate that the estimated models accurately reflect the high-frequency dynamics. Notably, the EM algorithm is efficient even with dense data, and the model parameters remain consistent across different sampling rates. Furthermore, the estimated cross-excitation parameters successfully capture dependencies between sources that simplified models fail to detect. The R package `mhpfit` can be downloaded from https://github.com/zhengyuxia/mhpfit.
