Our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshots of a dark matter-only simulation to forecast the halo mass of subsequent particles. Our findings indicate that while this method successfully identifies particles belonging to existing halos, it struggles with identifying new particles that collapse into halos. To address this challenge, we propose a modification to the CNN architecture that incorporates velocity and density information at each step, which significantly enhances the algorithm's performance. This improved technique allows for the identification of newly formed halos and results in a halo mass function that aligns well with historical measurements, provided that boundary conditions are managed appropriately. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating velocity and density data helps overcome issues arising from periodic boundary conditions, a finding that can be applied to accelerate traditional $F^{n}$-tree algorithms for calculating the halo mass function. Additionally, this deep learning method can serve to track the evolution of clusters of galaxies. Ultimately, this framework represents a versatile and robust tool for analyzing and following dark matter evolution, provided that initial conditions are well-resolved. Consequently, this implementation is applicable to various scenarios, including the investigation of how neutrinos impact small-scale structures. The code is available at: https://github.com/ahmedshoukry/DeepHaloMassFunction. Key components of this implementation are: velocity ($v$), density ($\rho$), and boundary conditions. Similar to reference [1], this approach leverages CNNs to track the evolution of dark matter and estimate the halo mass function. While traditional methods rely on identified particles (those already within a halo), our technique utilizes particles that were initially outside the halo region. By integrating velocity and density, the algorithm's accuracy is markedly improved. Although this method is trained on simulation particles, it is also effective for exploring structure formation in astrophysical observations. The proposed algorithm is not limited to calculating the halo mass function; it can also follow the evolution of clusters of galaxies and other related phenomena. Moreover, this technique is general-purpose and can be utilized to reduce computation times in conventional halo finding algorithms, as they often serve as a bottleneck in $N$-body simulations. Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike the standard Eulerian approach, this formulation solves force balance equations to determine the positions of fluid elements mapped to grid points. Distinct from prior literature, we do not rely on the first integral of the Euler equation, which typically lacks a general analytic solution. Instead of prescribing the spatial distribution of angular velocity or angular momentum as previous methods do, we assign specific mass, angular momentum, and entropy to each fluid element; the angular velocity and momentum distributions are subsequently derived once the positions of all elements are established. We discretize the time-independent Euler and Einstein equations using the finite-element method, resulting in a large system of nonlinear algebraic equations that we solve via our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. To validate this formulation, we have constructed both barotropic and baroclinic rotational configurations and solved three evolutionary sequences that simulate cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion as simplified toy models. Our findings indicate that this Lagrangian method offers significant advantages for evolutionary simulations, primarily due to the finite-element framework, which avoids artificial boundaries between computational cells, and the direct mapping of fluid elements to grid points, which eliminates the need for complex boundary conditions and data interpolation. Consequently, this formulation is ideally suited for evolutionary simulations, as the positions of individual fluid elements can be tracked to compute physical quantities such as luminosity, mass loss, and accretion rates. Furthermore, the system's robustness and efficiency make it a powerful tool for investigating astrophysical systems. To facilitate this, the code is now available for download. This study examines the DWD system properties alongside their observational limits across the GW, electromagnetic (EM), and astroseismic spectra. We investigate the feasibility of measuring G-K and late M main sequence DWDs via electromagnetic or astroseismic signals using current and future telescopes. By integrating DWD signals from these three domains, we can broaden the parameter coverage for GW observations, enhance measurements for systems detectable in EM or astroseismic light, or, in specific instances, enable the determination of masses and spins for DWDs that are not directly observable in EM or astroseismic spectra. Utilizing the GW catalog and signals from various detectors and EM/astroseismic instruments, we apply the Fisher approximation to evaluate detection probabilities and signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). Our findings indicate that the GW catalog can be supplemented with approximately 10% of system parameters using EM data and nearly 50% with astroseismic data. While enhancing measurements for detectable DWDs improves parameter resolution by up to six orders of magnitude for GWs and three orders of magnitude for EM, future detectors such as AEDGE, DECIGO, or TianGrang-3 would significantly amplify these effects. These results are particularly relevant for pulsar timing arrays and fast radio transients searches within the DWD population. Furthermore, the precise parameters of DWDs are crucial for testing modified gravity theories, studying dark matter, and analyzing neutron star mergers and their remnants. To achieve this, the DWD population must be expanded, which can be accomplished by leveraging signals from multiple spectral domains. Although EM and astroseismic detections are somewhat slower than GW detections, these methods are not constrained by the source redshift. With advanced technology, we can detect DWDs from EM and astroseismic signals that are invisible to GW observatories, thereby expanding the detectable parameter space and, in some cases, achieving precision comparable to GW measurements. These capabilities will be markedly improved with next-generation detectors like AEDGE, DECIGO, or TianGrang-3. Keywords: white dwarfs, gravitational waves, detectors, data analysis. This study introduces a framework for embedding interactions within a graph representation of urban spaces, where locations and amenities function as nodes and the frequencies of joint visits between them define the weights of connecting edges. This approach facilitates the identification of highly interconnected locations and clusters of places that foster frequent social activity. Furthermore, the framework quantifies the "interaction beta" divergence of geographic areas by comparing their local network structures against the overall urban network structure. When applied to smartphone location data from Los Angeles County, this method reveals distinct demographic and socioeconomic variations in interaction patterns across the region. These findings suggest that planning decisions and targeted interventions can be guided by a deeper understanding of how different areas of place vary in their capacity to support physical interactions. This framework is designed to be adaptable to diverse contexts and data sources, potentially offering insights into markets influenced by face-to-face interactions, such as those affected by pandemic-related restrictions. Urban physical interactions and social engagements play a pivotal role in fueling economic development and innovation while bolstering community strength and stability. Although their positive impacts are well-documented, systematically measuring them remains challenging. To address this gap, we present a framework for embedding interactions into graph representations of urban spaces, leveraging mobile device data. This process involves treating places and amenities as nodes, with edge weights representing the propensity of users to visit pairs of locations together. This configuration highlights clusters of places that actively facilitate frequent physical interactions among users. Additionally, we quantify the "interaction beta" divergence of geographic areas by contrasting their local network structure with the city-wide structure. Applications of this framework can guide planning decisions and targeted interventions designed to enhance place-based opportunities for physical interaction. Our results indicate that places in Los Angeles County serve as hubs for distinct demographic and socioeconomic interaction clusters, often differing significantly from the city's aggregate interaction profile. These findings demonstrate how empirical assessments of physical interaction potential across various geographic areas can harness the benefits derived from urban engagements. Moreover, this approach can be adapted to diverse contexts and data sources to examine markets shaped by face-to-face activities, including those impacted by pandemic restrictions.

By applying Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we simulate the evolution of these fields to determine the Gaussian curvature of the parametric space, examining its behavior across phase transitions. The simulations reveal an unexpected phenomenon termed the \emph{curvature effect}, signifying a pronounced asymmetric geometric deformation within the parametric space triggered by substantial fluctuations in the system's entropy. This approach offers a direct method to model non-equilibrium thermodynamic processes and investigates the arrow of time throughout the Markov process. Currently, this curvature approach is widely recognized as a cutting-edge method for analyzing irreversible processes and has been successfully deployed to study phenomena such as the arrow of time, the Lee-Yarrow theorem, and the breaking of time-reversal symmetry in various complex systems, including the spin-1/2 Heisenberg Hamiltonian, the Potts model, and Big Bang cosmology. $\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA) has demonstrated significant efficacy. This paper investigates the convex relaxation of L1-PCA through the lens of spectral theory. Specifically, the resulting uniform block diagonal (UBD) matrix derived from the spectral decomposition of this matrix is compared directly with the standard principal component (PC) loading vectors obtained via standard SVD. The findings reveal that the UBD matrix functions as a novel, effective estimator for data projection, offering a robust alternative to conventional SVD. These results provide a theoretical foundation for recent algorithms designed to solve the UBD matrix problem (e.g., GDS, RUP-UBD). Furthermore, the study establishes that this approach yields a significantly broader class of efficient algorithms for dimensionality reduction that are highly effective at identifying and handling outliers. This class encompasses not only existing methods like L1-PCA, sparse PCA (SPCA), and robust SVD (R-SVD), but also a wide variety of their hybrids and novel algorithms. These robust dimensionality projection methods are characterized by the following features: (1) they are exceptionally effective at detecting and managing both missing data and outliers; (2) they represent the first optimization paradigm capable of addressing the simultaneous challenges of missing data and outliers, which previous methods could not handle separately; and (3) the associated algorithms are extremely fast, executing in linear time relative to the number of data points. The proposed paradigm encompasses a vast range of missing-data robust PC loading vectors, including sparse, non-sparse, diagonal-regularized, group-structured (G-SPCA), and other advanced variants, all of which are optimal for datasets with missing entries and outperform state-of-the-art algorithms. Additionally, a fast, straightforward, and powerful algorithm for missing-data robust projection based on G-SPCA loading vectors is introduced. Finally, the spectrum of data types beneficially served by this robust projection framework—including data with missing values, data contaminated with outliers (both additive and multiplicative), and complex, non-linear datasets—is highlighted. Empirical results from multiple large-scale experiments confirm the accuracy and speed of these algorithms, demonstrating their superiority over current state-of-the-art techniques across various missing-data percentages and outlier scenarios (additive and multiplicative). Dialogue Act (DA) classification is fundamental to understanding and generating dialogue. Current approaches typically train classifiers using hand-crafted features extracted from annotated data. In this work, we utilize the word-level representations from a pre-trained Neural Language Model (NLM) to create a new feature set derived from rich linguistic features, which effectively captures both local and global semantic aspects of utterances. We evaluate our framework using two widely accepted DA classification datasets. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-line methods. Additionally, our framework is designed to be domain-agnostic and adaptable to various annotation schemas. System code and annotations are publicly available at https://github.com/aminreza00/DC-NLM.

Subsequently, a simple classifier infers the semantic class by integrating these lexical mappings with distributional semantic features. Experiments conducted on two dialogue act annotation datasets yield results that exceed state-of-the-line performance

While most existing map representations depend on drift-free state estimation to generate global metric maps, maintaining such consistency and speed is challenging in large-scale real-world scenarios. This paper introduces HiTMap, a novel representation designed to improve upon current methods. Its core concept involves utilizing a submap-based hierarchical topology instead of a global metric map, thereby maintaining multiple local metric maps for environmental reconstruction. The 'Hi' in HiTMap signifies its hierarchical structure, and the representation maintains two levels: at the upper level, a  graph captures the topological relationships and global geometry via nodes (corresponding to submaps) and edges (capturing relative geometry); at the lower level, each node hosts a local metric map for detailed reconstruction. This dual-level approach balances efficiency with accuracy, enabling efficient exploration of vast unknown environments while ensuring high-fidelity mapping of frequently traversed areas. We implemented HiTMap in a SLAM system using a real-time camera-mojo odometry estimator. Experimental results across both indoor and large-scale outdoor unknown environments demonstrate that the system achieves drift-free global mapping, real-time performance, and a high level of detail. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. Additionally, we report on a proposed method to measure the depth of the Meissner effect in superconducting films using atomic interference. Additionally, we suggest a protocol to discern between type I and type II superconductors based on the same expelled local magnetic field and its orientation relative to the film. Finally, we present estimation formulas for the sensitivity of the proposed experimental arrangement. The proposed setup relies on well-established phenomena and mature technologies, including the Meissner effect, the Mach-Zehnder interferometric effect, atomic gravity sensing, atomic diffraction, and the Josephson effect. Consequently, this research contributes to novel experimental methods for investigating type I and II superconductors and their fundamental properties. The primary objective is to precisely determine the magnetic field expelled by a superconductor, estimated at $1.1 \times 10^{-4}$ T, using Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry to sense the acceleration caused by magnetic field gradients in front of the superconductor. This approach enables the evaluation of the Meissner effect depth in superconducting films and allows researchers to identify whether a sample is type I or type II based on the field's expulsion characteristics. Furthermore, the experiment can assess the orientation of the expelled field (perpendicular or parallel to the film) to estimate the critical current density of type II superconductors. Because the experiment utilizes the Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometric effect to detect minute magnetic field gradients and employs atomic diffraction to place atoms above or below the sample, it offers high sensitivity and accurate measurement of critical current density. Thus, this method is anticipated to be broadly applicable in evaluating Type II superconducting films and their critical current density. Keywords: Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry, Meissner effect, type I and type II superconductors, critical current density, expelled local magnetic field, Meissner effect depth, superconducting films,

This paper addresses the question of determining the maximum value of $\lambda$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ guarantees a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor with upper density at least $\lambda \cdot \delta(V(F))$, where $\delta(V(F))$ denotes the minimum degree of $F$. We establish that $\lambda=1/2$ is optimal for any fixed graph $F$. Furthermore, for the specific case where $F$ is an odd cycle, we prove that $\lambda=2/(|V(F)|+1)$ is optimal. For general factors $F$, we demonstrate that $\lambda=2/(\pi(F)+1)$ is optimal, where $\pi(F)$ represents the nullity of $F$, defined as $\pi(F)=|V(F)|-e(F)+1+ \beta(F)$, with $\beta(F)$ being the smallest non-negative integer for which $e(F)-\beta(F)+1 \geq |V(F)|-\beta(B)$ holds for every bipartite subgraph $B$ of $F$. Additionally, we provide an alternative proof for the optimal bound of $1/2$ when $F$ is an odd cycle, utilizing a variant of the Komlós anti-Ramsey lemma. Our main findings also extend to the context of Turán numbers. Our proofs rely on infinite versions of Szemerédi's regularity method and a dynamical approach to amenability. The resulting bound for odd cycles is optimal up to a factor of $2$, while the bound for general factors is strictly optimal. This result for general graphs improves upon the finding by Montellano-Ballesteros and Rosales (2015), who showed $\lambda=2/(\pi(F)+2)$ is sufficient. The factor of $2$ discrepancy in the odd cycle case arises because our main lemma does not fully optimize the application of Kőnig's infinite version of the Hall marriage theorem. The optimization of $\lambda$ for general factors is achieved by carefully selecting subsets to apply this lemma.

Recent work by Boyer et al. demonstrates that for any $\epsilon$-accurate algorithm using qubits subject to depolarizing noise, the scaling of circuit depth with precision is limited by a constant, approximately $10^4$. Additionally, for a specific ansatz in 1+1 dimensional QED, accuracy loss due to decoherence scales linearly with circuit depth and noise strength when using qudits, scaling far more favorably than in qubit implementations. Our analysis of mass gap calculations in free QED reveals that while qudit simulations are linearly affected by both circuit length and noise strength, the feasibility of these simulations extends to much longer distances compared to qubit simulations. We demonstrate that utilizing a circularly polarized intense laser, a magnetized solid, and a electron-positron collider-yielded positrons with an expected average polarization exceeding 99%. Leveraging a collimated beam and a high asymmetry in momentum distribution, only modest total numbers of positrons are required to achieve this polarization level. Achieving this result required extending the QED calculation framework to include positron collider yield and momentum characteristics, alongside incorporating spin-dependent laser-solid annihilation dynamics into a two-step Monte Carlo simulation. These findings provide substantial advantages for preparing polarized positrons using accessible technological resources. Consequently, this approach is particularly beneficial for current and upcoming large-scale facilities, such as determining the hadron weak mixing angle through electron-positron scattering on solid deuterium or performing precision experiments on positronium. Furthermore, this generation method enables a rapid determination of the positron's anomalous magnetic moment. Our proposed scheme relies on relatively few assumptions and clearly outlines the underlying theoretical framework, allowing for an easy verification against existing theoretical predictions of collider yields, momentum distributions, and polarization. The estimated physical quantities were derived based on parameters from the HELICOS design report, although other high-power laser facilities can also achieve similar outcomes. Our findings indicate that a collider producing approximately $10^9$ positrons with an average polarization greater than 99% can be realized using a 100 TW laser within a few months. Consequently, the HELICOS facility is now considered feasible, and we urge the HELICOS collaboration to incorporate positron polarization into their design specifications to accelerate future experiments. This report comprehensively outlines the theoretical underpinnings, numerical methodologies, and theoretical framework expansion required to verify our claims. Ultimately, our results establish that the HELICOS facility can produce highly polarized positrons within a short timeframe, representing a significant advancement over current technological capabilities.

set $S \subseteq G$, the diameter $diam(G,S)$ denotes the smallest integer $n$ such that every element of $G$ can be expressed as a product of at most $n$ elements from $S$. In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes. These results generalize previous work by Breuillard, Guralnick, and TZAFARIS. Applications include providing bounds on the diameter of groups acting transitively on sets, conjugacy class numbers for groups acting faithfully on sets, and the number of irreducible representations for such groups. Regarding the bound for $|G|$ in terms of $diam(G,S)$ and $|S|$, our result is optimal up to the constant in the exponent; similarly, for the bound on the number of conjugacy classes, optimality holds when $G$ is simple. If the group $A$ mentioned in our main theorem is required to be characteristic, the bound on $|G|$ improves to $|A||S|^{O(log|S|)}$. Furthermore, if $S$ is a generating set of group elements that includes the identity, our bound becomes $O(log|S|)$. Regarding the specific case where the diameter is quadratic, we prove it is exactly so for groups with a large abelian section and slightly more general scenarios. Regarding the statement of our main theorem, our current formulation is not optimal; however, we have demonstrated that the structural description of groups with polynomial diameter can be significantly refined. Groups satisfying this improved description will be essential for deriving a bound on the number of irreducible representations, a task addressed in a separate paper. Finally, our bounds for the number of conjugacy classes and irreducible representations are approximately $22$ and $24$, respectively; these can be potentially lowered to $20$ and $22$ using the updated diameter bound for quadratic groups. Groups with polynomial diameter find applications in various fields, including the study of random walks, the classification of groups with a large number of conjugacy classes or irreducible representations, the analysis of mixing times, and the dynamics of group actions

Together, these chapters illustrate how to construct geometric structures on Homeo(X), T(X), and Vec(X).

an elastic membrane separating two fluids of differing densities during extrusion from beneath a rigid obstacle. The membrane's response to imbalanced forces on either side causes it to buckle and form folds that interact with the obstacle, creating a complex feedback loop between hydrodynamics and elasticity. By combining quantitative experimental observations with a linear stability analysis of periodic Bénard–Taylor fingers, we develop an instability diagram based on the threadable Hookean model. This model characterizes the membrane's shape using the buckling and stretching of the portion attached to the obstacle, accounting for surface tensions derived from the balance between bulk and interfacial pressures. The results indicate multiple buckling and stretching regimes for the obstacle-attached segment, yielding a series of bifurcations and periodic patterns as flow rate increases. Furthermore, the buckling behavior of the remaining membrane portion is governed by a effective surface tension, which can be either enhanced or reduced relative to the tension from the threadable Hookean model, depending on the flow rate and the membrane's intrinsic material properties. These findings are directly relevant to engineering applications involving elastic interfaces, such as oil recovery processes and microfluidic membrane pumps.

Translation (NMT), directing the translation process by selectively attending to specific parts of the source sentence during the prediction of each target word. However, we observe that generating a target word relies not only on the source input but also heavily on previously generated target words, particularly distant ones that recurrent neural networks struggle to model effectively. To address this, we introduce a novel look-ahead attention mechanism designed to directly capture dependencies between target words. Additionally, we devise three integration patterns to incorporate this mechanism into conventional attention models. Experiments conducted on Chinese-to-English (NIST) and English-to-German (WMT) translation tasks demonstrate that our proposed look-ahead attention mechanism yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved state-of-the-art results, yet the model remains a black box, making it difficult to comprehend the attention connections linking source words to target word generation. This paper presents a target-bigram attention model designed to capture bigram statistics within the target language. Furthermore, we offer an in-depth analysis of attention mechanisms using a target-bigram model across two datasets, revealing distinct attention patterns when modeling long-term dependencies within target sentences. Finally, we apply this mechanism in set-based NMT and sequence-to-sequence settings, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the WMT14 NMT task. Attention entropy analysis further indicates that the model captures different types of dependencies in both datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/yanan0627/Look-ahead-Attention-Mechanism-for-NMT.

Machine translation has seen significant advancements with the rise of deep learning, largely driven by the encoder-decoder architecture. Despite this progress, existing models often struggle to accurately capture dependencies among target words, as their capacity is limited by the sequence length of decoded outputs. To mitigate this, we propose a Set-based Neural Machine Translation approach that encodes generated target words into two distinct vectors: one representing the entire target set and another focusing on the most relevant source words for translation. Experimental results on WMT14 tasks show that our method surpasses the standard encoder-decoder model, and an ablation study confirms the individual value of both encoding components. Our code is hosted at: https://github.com

Biomedical engineers now leverage extensive knowledge of pathophysiology and materials science to create novel platforms for diagnosing and treating patients. While these developments hold significant potential, they must undergo rigorous testing to ensure safety and efficacy before becoming established clinical tools. Although laboratory settings offer numerous advantages for assessing biomedical devices, ensuring patient privacy remains a significant challenge when utilizing real patient data. BioAC Tomography (BAT) overcomes this privacy limitation by employing private, de-identified biometric data from recorded video feeds. This method utilizes the distinctive and permanent biometric signatures found in retinal blood vessel patterns to generate high-resolution, MRI and X-ray equivalent tomographic images of living subjects. Because BAT requires no training, no invasive procedures, and no administered materials, it is ideally suited for a broad spectrum of patients, including newborns, pediatric patients, and individuals who are obese, pregnant, or experience motion artifacts. This paper presents the design, development, and evaluation of a BAT system implemented on an open-source biomedical engineering platform. Furthermore, it outlines a private deep learning framework trained on BAT-generated images to demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing high-resolution X-ray equivalent tomographic visuals from BAT data. Finally, the paper demonstrates reconstructing high-resolution 3D X-ray equivalent tomographic images from BAT system recordings using a different, private deep learning system. The adiabatic segment allows the equation of state to asymptotically approach two distinct power laws, effectively interpolating between dust and dark energy regimes at early and late cosmic epochs. The dissipative component features a bulk viscosity with a constant coefficient. Utilizing phase space analysis, we robustly characterize the model's dynamical behavior without relying on explicit system solutions. Furthermore, the $Om(z)$ test confirms that, despite being quintessence-like, the model traverses the phantom barrier. Consequently, this approach avoids such a singularity. Compared to similar models fitted to similar data, ours exhibits lower chi-square values and lies closer to the $\Lambda$CDM trajectory in the $\{r,s\}$ plot.

—defined as the likelihood that the fraction of time up to $t$ during which a random walk $S$ with i.i.d. zero-mean increments (taking finitely many values) remains non-negative exceeds $x$ for all $s \in [1,t]$—decays according to the power law $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b,a)/2}$. Here, the exponent $\phi$ is determined by the walk's characteristics at the origin (specifically, the probabilities of taking negative or zero steps) and the parameters $t$, $x$, and the endpoints of the interval $[1,t]$. The functions $\phi$ and $a$ satisfy a second-order non-linear PDE, while $\phi$ satisfies a third-order non-linear PDE. Finite time $t$ considerations can be disregarded when $x=1$. Furthermore, we provide precise asymptotics for $\phi$ as $t \to \infty$ for values of $x$ that are $o(1)$ or $1+o(1)$, and we introduce an explicit formula for $\phi$ when the interval is $[0,t]$. Numerical evaluations of $\phi$ reveal that for typical increments, $\phi \approx 0.438$, yielding the asymptotic relation $p(t,x) \sim c x^{-0.876} t^{-0.562}$. These findings generalize previous results by Shepp and Louchard concerning the power-law decay of the probability that a random walk's entire trajectory up to time $t$ is non-negative, and of the fraction of time the walk is non-negative, given it is so at time $t$. Additionally, we offer refined asymptotics for $\phi$ and $a$ over specific ranges of $x$ and $t$, and we exactly characterize $\phi$ for $x=1/2$ and $1$. Finally, we discuss implications regarding the typical magnitude of the maximum of such a random walk. This research extends prior work by [15], which examined the probability that the maximum of a random walk with non-positive drift is only moderately larger than zero. Similar analyses can be conducted for random walks possessing non-negative drift.

This paper presents a theoretical investigation of the IShTAR ICRF system, focusing on the fast wave's behavior at the ion-cyclotron resonance. Specifically, it examines how quasi-perpendicular resonance conditions give rise to a magnetic field hill structure around the gyro-orbit, which enables the acceleration of ions to electrostatic ion-cyclotron harmonic frequencies. Additionally, the study explores the impact of ion-cyclotron harmonic number, magnetic field gradients, maximum magnetic field strength, and plasma frequency on the acceleration of ions to these high energies. Finally, the simulated outcomes are directly compared with recent experimental data obtained from the IShTAR device. Recent findings indicate that ions can be accelerated to approximately 2,-fold cyclotron energies, which aligns with theoretical predictions. However, recent updates to the experimental analysis suggest that cyclotron harmonic number three might also be achievable, a result that corroborates our current findings. To address these issues, deep learning techniques have been developed to automate cancer detection and evaluate histological features linked to clinical outcomes. Nevertheless, the effective deployment of these methods is hindered by the high cost and complexity associated with acquiring high-throughput, whole-slide imaging. To overcome this, intelligent multi-scale analysis has been proposed to synthesize lower-resolution megapixel images from strategically selected high-resolution image patches. This approach aims to create cancer-specific datasets featuring both raw and modeled whole-slide images, incorporating synthetic artifacts designed to test the robustness of deep learning classifiers. Ultimately, the goal is to develop and validate advanced cancer phenotyping tools capable of extracting biologically and clinically significant histological insights across entire tissue slides. Recently, the multi-resoluton whole-slide analysis (MORPHA) framework was introduced to achieve these objectives. However, MORPHA's capabilities regarding the generation of realistic composite whole-slide images and the use of state-of-the-deep learning classifiers for their analysis remain untested. This study investigates MORPHA's performance with realistic composite whole-slide images using state-of-the-art deep learning classifiers. We find that MORPHA currently lacks optimal strategies for selecting low-resolution image patches, a issue we attempt to resolve using simple, rule-based methods. Ultimately, we propose an optimized version of MORPHA, termed eMORPHA, which integrates hypergraph-based feature learning to extract low-resolution image patches. With eMORPHA, we demonstrate that the accuracy of classifying composite whole-slide images can approach that of high-grade component image patches, representing an improvement of over 10% F1 score compared to MORPHA. Furthermore, we show that the image regions corresponding to the component image patches in our composite whole-slide images can be identified using deep learning-based "attention maps." These attention mechanisms align with historical human-based findings, highlighting the most diagnostically relevant histological regions within whole-slide images. The eMORPHA framework is available at https://sites.google.com/view/emorpha.

This work revisits GCNN operations to demonstrate that their convolution layers function as matched filters, aligning input data with specific patterns or features. By adopting this matched filter perspective, we offer a unified explanation of GCNNs, extending the framework to include nonlinear ReLU and max-pooling layers. coupled to a scalar field featuring a two-parameter Higgs-like self-interaction is reformulated using a Chern-Simons form associated with the algebra $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$. Depending on the sign of the self-interaction couplings, the components $g^{\pm}$ correspond to $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$, or $iso(2,1)$. The field equations are expressed via the field strength of non-flat composite gauge fields, allowing conserved charges to be derived from boundary terms in the action. These charges align with standard pure gravity Chern-Simons theory but utilize non-flat connections. Field regularity is ensured by requiring trivial holonomy of the connections along contractible cycles; this condition is naturally satisfied by scalar solitons. Consequently, the Hawking temperature and chemical potential for rotating hairy black holes can be recovered, and their entropy is calculated using the same formula applicable to pure Chern-Simons theory. Additionally, within the conformal (Jordan) frame, the theory represents General Relativity with a cosmological constant conformally coupled to a self-interacting scalar field, and its description via a Chern-Simons form for appropriately constructed composite gauge fields is also briefly discussed. Finally, the field regularity condition translates into a non-trivial constraint on the boundary data, implying a bound on the angular velocity of rotating black holes, a feature with no analogue in the conformal (Jordan) formulation. The self-consistency of this approach is validated by being able to derive the entropy of (extremal) hairy black holes using the Noether charge method with the same self-interacting field. This confirms that the theory retains its minimality and can encompass black hole solutions with non-trivial hair, as long as the condition of regularity is defined via the triviality of the connection's holonomy rather than the smoothness of the metric. Consequently, the holographic dual of this theory could exhibit conformal field theory-like behavior at high energies while potentially displaying conformal symmetry breaking at low energies.

Although elastography can measure displacement both axially and laterally, axial estimates are superior due to higher sampling rates, resolution, and the presence of a strong carrier signal. In contrast, lateral estimates are often inferior, particularly when sample rates are low, resolution is high, the signal-to-noise ratio is poor, or apodization is used to avoid range aliasing. To address this, we propose a novel approach to enhance lateral displacement estimation. The method involves sampling at non-axial angles, where the effective sample rate and resolution are increased due to oblique propagation through the medium. This allows for more accurate displacement estimation. Finally, the results from all oblique samples are combined using beamforming to produce a high-quality axial displacement estimate. Simulation results, as well as measurements from phantom and biological samples, demonstrate that the proposed method significantly enhances lateral displacement estimation, confirmed by high-quality elastography images.

While WN, a probabilistic autoregressive model utilizing stacked dilated convolutions, excels at high-fidelity audio synthesis, its reliance solely on data without prior audio knowledge hampers its ability to control pitch. These boundaries classify the shadow's 1-morphisms, which in turn classify its coefficients; this hierarchical classification extends to coefficients defined on an arbitrary bicategory. The provided framework utilizes bounded 2-exact sequences, a approach favored in algebraic topology due to its compatibility with long exact sequences. Specifically, we employ two types of bounded 2-exact sequences: those containing a split exact sequence (characteristic of conflation bicategories) and those lacking one (general 2-exact sequences). For bounded 2-exact sequences without a split exact component, the resulting category is denoted as \textbf{Shad}_1, as its objects form a stable category that admits only trivial autoequivalences of the shadow. Conversely, bounded 2-exact sequences that include a split exact sequence are characterized by a short 2-exact sequence in their coefficients. The category \textbf{Shad}_2 comprises 2-exact bicategories, defined as those equivalent to conflation bicategories via their boundary and coefficient functors. It is demonstrated that \textbf{Shad}_1 is equivalent to \textbf{Shad}_2, a result that implies the 2-of-3 property for 2-exact bicategories. Furthermore, the paper explores the relationship between shadows and the long exact sequence associated with nucleations, and examines the connection between 2-exact and conflation bicategories in the context of the Gluing Lemma for morphisms and functors. Finally, the findings indicate that, similar to how conflation categories generalize short exact sequences, both shad_1 and shad_2 categories serve to generalize conflation categories.

Explicit methods for optimizing quadratic programs (QPs) typically struggle with large-scale problems, whereas scalable implicit approaches often sacrifice solution accuracy. This paper proposes a robust, scalable framework for solving QPs that integrates global optimality, substantial speedups, and solution accuracy. The proposed approach introduces two innovations: a novel feasibility pump and an adaptive stepsize strategy for the ellipsoid method. Our experiments show that the framework efficiently solves QPs ranging from hundreds to millions of variables. Source code is available at http://www.cs.bilkent.edu.tr/~diletsch/qps/. We introduce a new class of algorithms designed to solve convex optimization problems where the objective function is the maximum of several convex functions and subject to simple constraints. These methods are especially effective for structured problems, such as those with linear equality or inequality constraints. The algorithm achieves global linear convergence using only first-order information when paired with an appropriate stepsize selection rule. By integrating advanced techniques from machine learning, our approach attains constant-time complexity for large-scale linearly constrained quadratic programs (QCPLCs). For other large-scale constrained QCPLCs and problems with a finite number of convex components, the algorithm displays superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Source code is hosted at http://www.cs.bilkent

However, the application of GCNs is constrained by the high computational cost associated with their matrix multiplication operations, a problem that intensifies with larger adjacency matrices. Although approximate GCNs (AGCNs) were introduced to reduce complexity, their performance remains limited, and existing methods still rely on simplified adjacency matrix computations. Furthermore, the core architecture of the AGCN, which utilizes a global average pooling layer, restricts its effectiveness in certain scenarios. To address these challenges, this paper first proposes a approximate adjacency matrix designed to more accurately preserve the original matrix's characteristics. Leveraging this innovation, we introduce a simplified AGCN architecture that enhances performance beyond current standards. Our method achieves a linear time complexity of $O(N)$. Second, we propose three novel approximate attention mechanisms that exceed the capabilities of traditional global average pooling. We validate the effectiveness of our approach across two datasets: a word-level dataset (WikiWords) and a character-level dataset (WikiCharacters). To the best of our knowledge, our simplified AGCN architecture with the approximate adjacency matrix achieves the lowest time complexity while maintaining competitive performance. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that the proposed attention mechanisms yield superior results in the context of WikiWords. Finally, our attention mechanisms show promising outcomes when applied to named entity recognition (NER). Upon implementing this condition via the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure, the resulting gauge-fixed action retains a dependence on a single gauge parameter. This indicates that the harmonic gauge represents a family of conditions rather than a unique one. This perspective provides a physical justification for covariant harmonic gauges, which arise when a mass term is introduced for the gravitational perturbation. Specifically, selecting a particular harmonic gauge yields a theory of linearized massive gravity with the expected five degrees of freedom, successfully avoiding the vDVZ discontinuity that plagues the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the covariant harmonic gauge can be derived as the gauge condition in the St\"uckelberg formulation of massive gravity, ensuring the theory remains free of ghosts and avoiding the Boulware-Deser ghost. This approach also establishes a perturbative equivalence between the standard and St\"uckelberg formulations. Notably, the analysis reveals a direct link to Proca theory; by decoupling the trace component of the symmetric tensor, Proca theory emerges as a sub-theory within linearized massive gravity under harmonic gauge fixing. We support these findings with analysis of the propagators in both theories. These results have significant implications for understanding local gravitational modifications, as they suggest a general pathway to construct theories of linearized massive gravity without encountering the vDVZ discontinuity or the Boulware-Deser ghost. The proposed framework may be extended to non-linear theories, potentially offering an alternative to the ADM gauge used in D\'ejean-Tolley-Kosteleck\'y-Potting-Emerson gravity, while avoiding the issues associated with the St\"uckelberg approach. This work provides an introduction to recent literature on nonequilibrium negative temperature, aiming to encourage researchers in diverse fields to focus their future efforts on this captivating topic.

and analyzing multidimensional vectorial data. It processes "object-feature" data tables that include numerical values alongside textual labels for both rows (objects) and columns (features). The tool incorporates various statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), elastic maps (a non-linear PCA variant), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, and a decision tree algorithm variant. Featuring intuitive interfaces for customizing data point attributes (size, shape, color) and a rapid 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables users to build interactive 3D scenes representing data within multidimensional space. This allows for efficient and insightful statistical analysis, ranging from fundamental to sophisticated methods. Furthermore, the decision components of the embedded tree algorithm were adapted specifically for clustering purposes. To enhance accessibility, a Python library version of ViDaExpert is available to facilitate its integration into other projects. Given its versatile and efficient nature, the library has been adopted within this paper to implement standard and supervised statistical analyses, such as PCA, elastic map, and LDA, along with K-Means and hierarchical clustering algorithms.
